entries.principle: First impressions form fast and color later judgments
entries.claim: People form a stable opinion of a page's visual appeal after a glimpse of half a second or less. That opinion then colors their early judgments of trust and usability.
entries.mechanism: The eye takes in overall layout, color and density before it reads anything. That fast, feeling-based verdict then acts as a halo (one good or bad impression spilling over onto unrelated qualities), and people tend to notice evidence that confirms it.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the judgment happens before deliberate thought
effects.satisfaction: raises — when the first view looks ordered and appealing; lowers when it does not
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — appealing pages are expected to be easier before any use

designMoves: Treat the first viewport (what shows without scrolling) as the page that gets judged: one clear focal point, visible structure, nothing half-loaded.
Make the first paint complete: fonts, hero image and spacing must not visibly swap or jump after load.
Judge the first viewport at phone and desktop width, and in each theme offered.
Test the impression with a look of a few seconds by someone who has not seen the page.
antiPatterns: A first viewport that is mostly a cookie banner, a loader or a placeholder.
Polished inner pages behind a cluttered entry view.
Assuming a good first impression survives a broken task (see beauty-masks-only-minor-problems).

howToCheck.machine: Capture screenshots of the first viewport at first contentful paint and at load; compare them for layout shift and for overlays that cover more than a set share of the viewport.
howToCheck.human: Show the first viewport for a few seconds to someone unfamiliar with it. Ask what the page is, whether it looks trustworthy and what they would click.

evidence.strengthNote: Lindgaard et al. (2006) ran three lab studies with homepage screenshots; ratings after 50 ms and 500 ms correlated highly. Tractinsky et al. (2006) replicated with 40 participants and 50 pages and found ratings after 500 ms correlated highly with ratings after 10 s, with considerable individual differences. Lindgaard et al. (2011) found that 50 ms judgments of trust and usability were driven mostly by visual appeal. Sample sizes of the 2006 Lindgaard studies were not confirmed in this session. All stimuli were static screenshots rated by small samples; the studies measure the stability of a rating, not behavior on a live site.

sources.citation: Lindgaard, G., Fernandes, G., Dudek, C., & Brown, J. (2006). Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression! Behaviour & Information Technology, 25(2), 115-126.

Tractinsky, N., Cokhavi, A., Kirschenbaum, M., & Sharfi, T. (2006). Evaluating the consistency of immediate aesthetic perceptions of web pages. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 64(11), 1071-1083.

Lindgaard, G., Dudek, C., Sen, D., Sumegi, L., & Noonan, P. (2011). An exploration of relations between visual appeal, trustworthiness and perceived usability of homepages. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 18(1), Article 1.

entries.caveats: Stable is not the same as decisive: the studies show that the snap rating persists, not that it determines whether people stay, buy or succeed. After real use, usability changes the rating. Individual tastes differ widely.
entries.sleekRelevance: A refined look has to be present in the first rendered frame. Refinement that arrives after fonts swap or content jumps reads as unfinished.

entries.principle: Simple and typical beats busy and unusual at first sight
entries.claim: Pages with low visual complexity and high prototypicality (how much a page looks like what people expect for its type) receive the best first-impression ratings. Visual complexity matters more than colorfulness.
entries.mechanism: A simple, expected layout is quick for the visual system to process, and that ease itself feels pleasant (see processing-fluency-liking). Unusual or dense layouts cost effort before the visitor has a reason to spend it.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer and more expected elements to parse
effects.satisfaction: raises — higher appeal ratings on first view
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the page matches the visitor's template for that kind of site

designMoves: Keep the layout skeleton typical for the genre; spend distinctiveness on type, color, imagery and one signature element.
Limit the number of distinct text styles, colors and box treatments visible in one viewport.
Use one accent color for emphasis and keep the rest of the palette quiet.
Group content into a few clear regions instead of many small competing blocks.
antiPatterns: Many competing blocks, badges and colors above the fold.
An unconventional layout skeleton used only to look different.
Decoration added to a page that lacks hierarchy.

howToCheck.machine: Count distinct font sizes, weights, colors and bordered or shadowed containers in the first viewport. Use the compressed file size of a screenshot as a rough proxy for visual complexity. Compare each count with a threshold the Catalog sets; the research gives no universal cutoff.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether the page looks like the kind of site it is, and whether anything competes with the main message.

evidence.strengthNote: Tuch et al. (2012): study 1 used 119 website screenshots that varied in complexity and prototypicality; study 2 used exposures of 17, 33 and 50 ms. Complexity affected ratings even at 17 ms; prototypicality gained influence with longer exposure. Reinecke et al. (2013): 548 volunteers rated 450 sites after 500 ms; models of complexity and colorfulness, with demographics, explained about half of the variance in appeal, and complexity was the stronger predictor. Both rely on static screenshots and snap ratings.

sources.citation: Tuch, A. N., Presslaber, E. E., Stöcklin, M., Opwis, K., & Bargas-Avila, J. A. (2012). The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites: Working towards understanding aesthetic judgments. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 70(11), 794-811.
Google Research (2012). Users love simple and familiar designs - Why websites need to make a great first impression. Google Research blog.

Reinecke, K., Yeh, T., Miratrix, L., Mardiko, R., Zhao, Y., Liu, J., & Gajos, K. Z. (2013). Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics with a quantification of perceived visual complexity and colorfulness. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 2049-2058.

entries.caveats: The result describes averages: about half of the variance stays unexplained, and preferences differ by age, education and country (see preferences-vary-by-audience). 'Typical' is defined per genre and changes over time. Very low complexity can also look empty or cheap (see simplicity-can-read-as-cheap).
entries.sleekRelevance: Sleekness in this research is mostly subtraction: a conventional skeleton with few visual ingredients, each used consistently. The bespoke part must come from the quality of those few ingredients, not from more of them.

entries.principle: Folklore: 'you have 50 milliseconds to win the visitor'
entries.claim: The studies show that a visual-appeal rating formed in 50 ms agrees with the rating formed after longer viewing. They do not show that visitors decide to stay, trust or buy in 50 ms.
entries.mechanism: The claim is a headline taken from a paper title. The experiments flashed screenshots and asked for ratings; they did not measure behavior on live sites.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the claim concerns a rating, not effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the 50 ms studies did not measure satisfaction after use
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured in the 50 ms studies

designMoves: Use the finding for what it supports: make the first view orderly and appealing.
Do not trade task clarity or loading speed for first-glance spectacle on the strength of this claim.
When someone quotes the 50 ms figure as a conversion fact, ask which behavior was measured.
antiPatterns: Quoting '50 ms' as proof that visual polish outranks content and usability.
Heavy hero animation justified by first-impression statistics.

howToCheck.human: Check that any written rationale describes the finding as the stability of a rating, not as visitor behavior.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the popular generalization. The underlying research (Lindgaard et al., 2006; replication by Tractinsky et al., 2006) is peer-reviewed and sound, but it measured ratings of screenshots only.

sources.citation: Lindgaard, G., Fernandes, G., Dudek, C., & Brown, J. (2006). Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression! Behaviour & Information Technology, 25(2), 115-126.
Hopkin, M. (2006). Web users judge sites in the blink of an eye. Nature news, 13 January 2006.

entries.caveats: The opposite misreading is also wrong: first impressions do matter and they persist. They are not the whole decision. The title and byline of the Nature news item are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Guards against spending the whole craft budget on a splashy first frame.

entries.principle: Attractive interfaces are judged easier to use before use
entries.claim: Before people use an interface, they rate better-looking versions as easier to use, even when attractiveness has little to do with real ease of use.
entries.mechanism: With no experience to go on, people infer hidden qualities from visible ones. Beauty raises an overall sense that the product is good, and 'easy to use' is inferred from that overall judgment (a halo effect).

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — it changes expectations, not effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — early ratings and willingness to try
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — before use and during first contact

designMoves: Give first-run screens the same visual care as the marketing page, because the expectation of ease is set there.
Ask for the first small action while the positive expectation holds.
In user tests, record task success and time as well as ratings, because ratings of a polished design run high.
antiPatterns: Reading high ratings of a polished mock-up as proof that it is usable.
Unstyled first-run and empty states.

howToCheck.human: Compare ratings collected before use with task success during use. A large gap signals that looks are carrying the score.

evidence.strengthNote: Kurosu and Kashimura (1995) had participants rate 26 ATM screen layouts; apparent usability correlated with beauty (r about .59) and little with the designed-in usability factors (secondary sources disagree on the sample: 156 or 252). Tractinsky (1997) replicated the result in Israel with the same layouts. Tractinsky, Katz and Ikar (2000) found that the aesthetics of a simulated ATM affected post-use ratings of usability while actual usability did not. Hassenzahl and Monk (2010) reviewed 15 papers with 25 correlations and found that the size of the beauty-usability link varies widely and runs through an overall 'goodness' judgment. The early studies are old and used ratings of pictures or a single simulated device.

sources.citation: Kurosu, M., & Kashimura, K. (1995). Apparent usability vs. inherent usability: Experimental analysis on the determinants of the apparent usability. CHI '95 Conference Companion, 292-293.
Tractinsky, N. (1997). Aesthetics and apparent usability: Empirically assessing cultural and methodological issues. Proceedings of CHI '97, 115-122.
Tractinsky, N., Katz, A. S., & Ikar, D. (2000). What is beautiful is usable. Interacting with Computers, 13(2), 127-145.
Hassenzahl, M., & Monk, A. (2010). The inference of perceived usability from beauty. Human-Computer Interaction, 25(3), 235-260.

entries.caveats: The effect is strongest before use and when usability differences are small. See beauty-masks-only-minor-problems for when it fails or reverses. Page numbers of the 1995 and 1997 papers are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: A refined surface buys a short period of goodwill and patience. It is a loan that the first tasks repay or forfeit.

entries.principle: Beauty hides small usability problems, not large ones
entries.claim: After real use, usability drives ratings. Good looks soften minor friction early on, but they do not hide serious problems, and frustration lowers people's ratings of the looks themselves.
entries.mechanism: Experience replaces inference. Once people have tried the task, they judge from what happened. The emotion from a failed task (frustration) spreads to their view of the whole product, including its appearance.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — looks do not remove the effort of a hard task
effects.satisfaction: mixed — looks lift early ratings; failures pull all ratings down
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — raised before use, corrected by use

designMoves: Fix task-blocking problems before spending on polish; polish cannot compensate for them.
Check every primary task end to end on the rendered build, not only the look of each screen.
Re-test after several uses, because the advantage of good looks shrinks with experience.
antiPatterns: Shipping a beautiful flow with a broken or confusing step.
Answering usability complaints with a visual redesign.

howToCheck.machine: Run scripted primary tasks (for example with Playwright) and fail the build on blocked steps, dead controls or console errors, independently of visual checks.
howToCheck.human: Watch a first-time user attempt the main task without help. Note where they stop.

evidence.strengthNote: Tuch et al. (2012): 80 participants used one of four versions of an online shop (high or low aesthetics, high or low usability); aesthetics did not change perceived usability, while poor usability lowered post-use ratings of aesthetics. Minge and Thüring (2018): 60 participants with audio players; looks influenced perceived usability at first, and usability influenced perceived attractiveness later. Grishin and Gillan (2019): no effect of aesthetics on System Usability Scale ratings once usability was manipulated. Nielsen Norman Group (NN/g) reports the same boundary from its usability testing: a pretty design makes users forgive minor problems, not large ones. Each experiment is a single lab study with one product type.

sources.citation: Tuch, A. N., Roth, S. P., Hornbæk, K., Opwis, K., & Bargas-Avila, J. A. (2012). Is beautiful really usable? Toward understanding the relation between usability, aesthetics, and affect in HCI. Computers in Human Behavior, 28(5), 1596-1607.
Minge, M., & Thüring, M. (2018). Hedonic and pragmatic halo effects at early stages of user experience. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 109, 13-25.
Grishin, J., & Gillan, D. J. (2019). Exploring the boundary conditions of the effect of aesthetics on perceived usability. Journal of Usability Studies, 14(2), 76-104.
Moran, K. (2017). The aesthetic-usability effect. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: Results depend on how strong each manipulation was. With mild usability differences and brief use, the looks halo can still dominate ratings. The author and year of the NN/g article are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: A premium feel is the combination of refined looks and tasks that work. A failed task makes the same pixels look worse.

entries.principle: Attractive interfaces improve task performance slightly on average
entries.claim: Across experiments, better-looking interfaces produce a small to moderate gain in measured performance, with large differences between studies.
entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms: pleasant looks improve mood and motivation, so people persist longer; some aesthetic changes (typography, contrast) also make content easier to perceive. The meta-analyses cannot separate these.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — unclear whether gains come from lower effort or higher motivation
effects.satisfaction: raises — indirectly, through mood
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — the meta-analyses measured performance

designMoves: Treat visual quality as a modest aid to performance, not as decoration only.
Prefer aesthetic improvements that also aid perception: clear type, adequate contrast, orderly alignment.
Do not expect looks to rescue performance on a hard task.
antiPatterns: Claiming large productivity gains from a visual refresh.
Decorative effects that add clutter in the name of beauty.

howToCheck.human: Measure task time and success on the old and the new visual version of the same structure.

evidence.strengthNote: Thielsch, Scharfen, Masoudi and Reuter (2019): 25 studies, 101 effects, 3,025 participants; Hedges' g = 0.12, high heterogeneity, no significant moderators. Schlamann, Nestler and Thielsch (2026, preregistered): 31 studies, 234 effect sizes, 18,794 participants; g = 0.29 with high unexplained heterogeneity; typography manipulation and interaction device moderated the effect, and prior experienced usability may confound results. The 2026 figures come from the authors' supplementary record and a university press release, not from the journal page; the exact title and issue were not confirmed.

sources.citation: Thielsch, M. T., Scharfen, J., Masoudi, E., & Reuter, M. (2019). Visual aesthetics and performance: A first meta-analysis. Proceedings of Mensch und Computer 2019, 199-210.

Schlamann, Nestler, & Thielsch (2026). Attractive things do work better [meta-analysis of aesthetics and performance]. International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction. Supplementary record on Zenodo.
Sonderegger, A., & Sauer, J. (2010). The influence of design aesthetics in usability testing: Effects on user performance and perceived usability. Applied Ergonomics, 41(3), 403-410.

entries.caveats: High heterogeneity means some studies find no effect or a negative one. The influence of looks in one-off tests wanes with repeated use. Page numbers of the 2019 paper are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Supports the case that refinement is functional, but only modestly. The larger payoff of refinement is trust and willingness to engage.

entries.principle: What is easy to process is liked more
entries.claim: The more easily people can perceive and make sense of something, the more they like it. Symmetry, clear contrast between figure and background, repetition and familiar form all raise that ease.
entries.mechanism: Processing fluency is the felt ease of taking something in. The mind registers that ease as mildly pleasant, and people attribute the pleasant feeling to the thing itself. The same feeling transfers to judgments of effort: instructions printed in a hard-to-read font make the task seem harder.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fluent layouts take less effort to parse
effects.satisfaction: raises — ease is experienced as liking
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — ease of reading transfers to expected ease of doing

designMoves: Align elements to a shared grid and reuse the same spacing steps so the eye can predict where things are.
Keep clear contrast between content and background and between adjacent regions.
Repeat component shapes and treatments; do not restyle the same thing in different places.
Set instructions and form help in the most readable text style on the page.
Use balance (symmetry, or asymmetry anchored to a grid) instead of loose placement.
antiPatterns: Low-contrast text used for an elegant look.
Many one-off spacings and alignments.
Decorative display type for instructions or form labels.

howToCheck.machine: Measure text contrast ratios. Count distinct spacing values, font sizes and left-edge alignment positions; flag one-off values.
howToCheck.human: Squint test: with the page blurred, can the main regions and their order still be told apart?

evidence.strengthNote: Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman (2004) is a theory review that integrates many experiments on figural goodness, figure-ground contrast, repetition, symmetry and prototypicality. Song and Schwarz (2008) found that people expected a recipe to take longer and to need more skill when it was printed in a hard-to-read font (small student samples, one study with 19 participants; no direct replication was found in this session). Tuch, Bargas-Avila and Opwis (2010): 60 participants, 20 website start pages; vertical symmetry raised beauty ratings, but only among men.

sources.citation: Reber, R., Schwarz, N., & Winkielman, P. (2004). Processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure: Is beauty in the perceiver's processing experience? Personality and Social Psychology Review, 8(4), 364-382.
Song, H., & Schwarz, N. (2008). If it's hard to read, it's hard to do: Processing fluency affects effort prediction and motivation. Psychological Science, 19(10), 986-988.
Tuch, A. N., Bargas-Avila, J. A., & Opwis, K. (2010). Symmetry and aesthetics in website design: It's a man's business. Computers in Human Behavior, 26(6), 1831-1837.

entries.caveats: Fluency explains liking, not interest: very fluent designs can bore (see pleasure-interest-balance). The symmetry effect on websites appeared only for men in the one study that tested it. Fluency also makes statements feel truer, so it is a responsibility as well as a tool. Volume and pages of the Song and Schwarz paper are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Much of what people call 'clean' is measurable regularity: few spacing values, consistent alignment, clear contrast. Regularity is the cheapest route to a refined look.

entries.principle: Repetition increases liking, up to a point
entries.claim: Repeated exposure to a form increases liking at first; with more exposure liking levels off and then declines.
entries.mechanism: Each exposure makes the form easier to recognize and process, which feels pleasant. With too many exposures the form becomes tedious, and the pleasure turns into boredom.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — repeated patterns are recognized faster
effects.satisfaction: mixed — rises with familiarity, falls with saturation
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — familiar patterns feel self-evident

designMoves: Reuse a small set of patterns within a product so each becomes familiar quickly.
Borrow widely seen patterns for controls that people must operate without thinking.
For elements meant to carry identity, avoid the most over-used visual treatments of the moment.
antiPatterns: A new pattern for every screen.
Identity built entirely from the most common template look.

howToCheck.machine: Count distinct component variants per role (buttons, cards, inputs) across pages.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether the page looks like many others seen recently, and which element the viewer remembers.

evidence.strengthNote: Montoya, Horton, Vevea, Citkowicz and Lauber (2017): 268 curve estimates from 81 articles; a positive slope with a negative quadratic term, which is an inverted-U curve. The authors state that existing explanations do not fully account for the data. Stimuli are mostly simple laboratory items (shapes, words, faces), not interfaces. The original effect was reported by Zajonc (1968), cited from memory.

sources.citation: Montoya, R. M., Horton, R. S., Vevea, J. L., Citkowicz, M., & Lauber, E. A. (2017). A re-examination of the mere exposure effect: The influence of repeated exposure on recognition, familiarity, and liking. Psychological Bulletin, 143(5), 459-498.
Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 9(2, Pt. 2), 1-27.

entries.caveats: Where the peak lies for interface styles is unknown. The decline with over-exposure is one plausible reason heavily repeated looks start to read as generic, but that link is an inference, not a tested result.
entries.sleekRelevance: Explains both sides of the generic problem: common patterns feel easy, and the most repeated looks wear out. Use familiarity for function and something less worn for identity.

entries.principle: Easy feels pleasant; a small challenge that resolves feels interesting
entries.claim: Immediate ease produces pleasure, and for people motivated to look longer, a design that is slightly hard at first and then makes sense produces interest. A design that is too easy produces boredom, and one that never resolves produces confusion.
entries.mechanism: The Pleasure-Interest Model of Aesthetic Liking describes two stages: a fast, automatic stage rewards fluency; a slower, deliberate stage rewards the experience of reducing an initial difficulty.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — a deliberate, small increase can pay off; a large one does not
effects.satisfaction: mixed — pleasure from ease, interest from resolved novelty, boredom from total predictability
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — interest-raising elements must stay off the task path

designMoves: Keep task-critical parts (navigation, forms, primary actions) fully fluent.
Place one element that rewards a second look (an unusual type treatment, a distinctive illustration or layout move) where it blocks no task.
Make sure the unusual element resolves quickly: its purpose should be clear within a moment.
antiPatterns: Novel navigation or controls that must be figured out.
A page with no element that rewards attention.
Several competing unusual elements.

howToCheck.human: Ask a viewer what they remember a minute later and whether anything confused them. One remembered element and no confusion is the target.

evidence.strengthNote: Graf and Landwehr (2015) is a theoretical model published in a review journal. Their 2017 experiments found that disfluent product designs gained attractiveness through interest when people viewed them in a deliberate way. Tested mainly with product images, not interfaces. Independent tests exist but are few.

sources.citation: Graf, L. K. M., & Landwehr, J. R. (2015). A dual-process perspective on fluency-based aesthetics: The pleasure-interest model of aesthetic liking. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 19(4), 395-410.
Graf, L. K. M., & Landwehr, J. R. (2017). Aesthetic pleasure versus aesthetic interest: The two routes to aesthetic liking. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 15.

entries.caveats: Interest requires motivation and time; visitors in a hurry only get the first, fluency-driven stage. Transfer from product images to interfaces is assumed.
entries.sleekRelevance: This is the best available account of why template-like pages feel flat and why one deliberate signature element lifts a design without harming use.

entries.principle: 'Intuitive' means 'uses what the person already knows'
entries.claim: An interface feels intuitive when people can use it with knowledge they already have. Nothing is intuitive in itself; a design is intuitive for a given person with a given history.
entries.mechanism: People act by transferring skills from things they have used before. Spool's model names the 'knowledge gap': the distance between what a user already knows (current knowledge) and what the design requires (target knowledge). A design feels intuitive when the gap is zero, or when the design closes the gap without the user noticing.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no new rules to learn
effects.satisfaction: raises — success without effort
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — this is the definition of the feeling

designMoves: Name the audience and list the products they already use; take control patterns and words from those.
For each screen, write down what the user must know to succeed. Remove each requirement or teach it in place (a label, an example, a default).
Use standard controls for standard jobs: native inputs, ordinary links and buttons.
Where something new is necessary, teach it at the moment of use, not in a tour.
antiPatterns: Icon-only controls with no label for uncommon actions.
Invented terms for common concepts.
Custom widgets that replace familiar ones without added value.
Calling a design intuitive without naming for whom.

howToCheck.machine: Flag icon-only buttons without visible text. Flag custom elements that stand in for native controls (for example a div with a click handler and no role).
howToCheck.human: First-use test with a member of the audience: count the moments they stop to work out what something does.

evidence.strengthNote: Raskin (1994) is a one-page argument, not a study. Experimental support comes from Blackler, Popovic and Mahar (2003, 2010), who found that prior experience with similar features predicted faster and more intuitive use of new products; those two papers are cited from memory and were not re-checked in this session. Spool (2005) is a practitioner model based on observation in usability tests. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility (supplemental guidance, not a conformance requirement) recommends familiar design.

sources.citation: Raskin, J. (1994). Intuitive equals familiar. Communications of the ACM, 37(9), 17.
Spool, J. M. (2005). What makes a design seem 'intuitive'? User Interface Engineering (now Center Centre).
Blackler, A., Popovic, V., & Mahar, D. (2003). The nature of intuitive use of products: An experimental approach. Design Studies, 24(6), 491-506.
Blackler, A., Popovic, V., & Mahar, D. (2010). Investigating users' intuitive interaction with complex artefacts. Applied Ergonomics, 41(1), 72-92.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (pattern: familiar design). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: Familiarity is specific to an audience, and it shifts as popular products change. Familiar does not mean optimal: a better but unfamiliar design costs learning first.
entries.sleekRelevance: Refinement belongs in how a familiar control is drawn and behaves, not in replacing it. Sophisticated products look distinctive and still operate the way people expect.

entries.principle: Jakob's law: people expect your site to work like the others they use
entries.claim: People spend most of their time on other sites and apps, so they arrive with a mental model (an internal picture of how such things work and where things are). Designs that match the model are found and used faster.
entries.mechanism: A mental model lets people predict where to look and what will happen. When a page matches the prediction, no search or reasoning is needed. When it does not, people look in the expected place first and lose time.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — prediction replaces search
effects.satisfaction: raises — fewer wrong turns
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — things are where people look first

designMoves: Place common objects where the genre puts them. Typical examples in left-to-right languages: logo and home link at the top left, primary navigation across the top or in a left rail, search and account controls at the top right, legal and contact links in the footer.
Keep link and button behavior standard: links navigate, buttons act.
Check the expected positions for the genre (shop, news, company site, app) before departing from them.
When departing, limit the departure to one object and give it a strong signifier.
antiPatterns: Navigation hidden or moved for visual novelty.
A logo that does not link to the home page.
Search or cart placed in an unusual corner.

howToCheck.machine: Locate logo, primary navigation, search, account and cart by role and position; compare with the expected regions for the template family; verify that the logo links to the home page.
howToCheck.human: Ask a newcomer to find search, contact and the main product. Record the time to the first click.

evidence.strengthNote: The law is Jakob Nielsen's summary of NN/g usability testing, first stated around 2000 (cited from memory). Peer-reviewed support: Roth et al. (2010) found that users largely agree on where common web objects belong on online shops, news portals and company pages, and that these expectations are robust across demographic groups; a follow-up by Heinz and colleagues (2016) found that expectations had shifted for some objects. The sample size of Roth et al. was not confirmed in this session. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility lists familiar and consistent design as supplemental guidance.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (2000). End of web design. Nielsen Norman Group (Alertbox column in which the law was first stated).

Roth, S. P., Schmutz, P., Pauwels, S. L., Bargas-Avila, J. A., & Opwis, K. (2010). Mental models for web objects: Where do users expect to find the most frequent objects in online shops, news portals, and company web pages? Interacting with Computers, 22(2), 140-152.
Heinz, S., et al. (2016). Is it still where I expect it? Users' current expectations of interface elements on the most frequent types of websites. Interacting with Computers.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (patterns: familiar design, consistent design). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: Expectations are a moving target and differ by genre, device and region. Following convention gives ease, and it also makes a page resemble its peers; identity has to come from elsewhere.
entries.sleekRelevance: Conventions are the floor that lets visual sophistication be noticed for the right reasons. Breaking layout conventions is the least efficient way to look original.

entries.principle: People act on signifiers, and signifiers work because they are familiar
entries.claim: An affordance is an action that is possible; a signifier is a perceivable cue that tells people the action exists and where to perform it. On a screen, people can only act on signifiers, and most signifiers (underline, button shape, chevron, input border) work because people have learned them elsewhere.
entries.mechanism: Almost anything on a screen could respond to a click, so the possibility of action is invisible. A cue that matches a learned convention is recognized without thought. A cue that is weak, new or missing makes people look around, hesitate or miss the control.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no guessing about what is interactive
effects.satisfaction: raises — less hesitation and fewer missed controls
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — controls announce themselves in a known vocabulary

designMoves: Give every interactive element at least one strong, consistent signifier (fill, border, underline or a familiar control shape) that non-interactive elements never use.
Reuse the conventional signifier for each control type before inventing one.
Provide hover, focus and pressed states for every control.
Keep text that looks like a link a link, and leave text that is not a link unstyled.
When a flat or minimal style is chosen, keep one unmistakable cue per control.
antiPatterns: Ghost buttons or plain text as the primary action.
Headings or labels styled like links.
Interactive cards with no visible cue.
Translucent or low-contrast controls over busy content.

howToCheck.machine: For each focusable or clickable element, verify a visual difference from body text (background, border, underline or weight) and the presence of hover and focus styles. Flag non-interactive elements that use the link color.
howToCheck.human: Ask someone to point at everything they think they can click. Compare with the truth.

evidence.strengthNote: The concepts are Norman's (a scholarly book; a framework, not an experiment), known here through secondary descriptions. Behavioral support: an NN/g eyetracking study (2017; 71 users and 9 sites according to secondary coverage) compared pages with strong and weak clickability cues; pages with weak signifiers took 22% longer and drew 25% more fixations. NN/g notes that the slowdown for a whole task would often be smaller and that errors were not measured. One vendor study, not peer reviewed. The perception-cognition part of this knowledge base covers the same study in its entry 'weak-signifiers'.

sources.citation: Norman, D. A. (2013). The Design of Everyday Things (revised and expanded edition). Basic Books.
Meyer, K. (2017). Flat UI elements attract less attention and cause uncertainty. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: Experienced users of a known product tolerate flatter styling. The NN/g study removed cues from existing pages, so it shows the cost of weak cues, not a need for heavy three-dimensional styling. The author name of the NN/g article is recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Minimal styling reads as refined only while controls stay obvious. The refined solution is a restrained but unmistakable signifier system, not the removal of signifiers.

entries.principle: MAYA: most advanced, yet acceptable
entries.claim: People prefer designs that combine typicality (looking like a good example of its kind) with novelty. Each raises preference and each tends to suppress the other, so the best-liked designs are novel without ceasing to look typical.
entries.mechanism: Typicality gives ease and a sense of safety; novelty gives interest and relieves boredom. A more novel design usually looks less typical, so the preferred designs keep the recognizable structure of the category and change something else.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — typical parts lower it; the novel part raises it slightly
effects.satisfaction: raises — when both typicality and novelty are present
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — depends on where the novelty sits

designMoves: Decide which parts stay typical (structure, navigation, control behavior) and which one or two carry novelty (type, color, imagery, a signature element, motion).
Spend the novelty in one place that the visitor will notice and that no task depends on.
Check that the page is still recognizable as its genre at a glance.
antiPatterns: Novelty spread thinly over every element.
Novelty applied to the layout skeleton or to controls.
A fully typical page with nothing of its own.

howToCheck.machine: Count departures from the template defaults by category (layout, type, color, shape, motion). Flag zero departures. Flag departures in navigation or form controls.
howToCheck.human: Ask a newcomer two questions: what kind of site is this, and what is different about it? Both should have a quick answer.

evidence.strengthNote: Hekkert, Snelders and van Wieringen (2003) studied consumer products such as telephones, sanders and teakettles; typicality and novelty together explained a large share of aesthetic preference (a secondary summary reports 56%) and were about equally important. The suppression relationship is stated from memory of the abstract; later product-design studies report strong negative correlations between the two. The evidence concerns physical products; application to interfaces is by analogy, supported by the website prototypicality findings. The 'one place' rule is a design inference that practitioner guidance also recommends.

sources.citation: Hekkert, P., Snelders, D., & van Wieringen, P. C. W. (2003). 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design. British Journal of Psychology, 94(1), 111-124.

Tuch, A. N., Presslaber, E. E., Stöcklin, M., Opwis, K., & Bargas-Avila, J. A. (2012). The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 70(11), 794-811.
Anthropic (2026). frontend-design skill (SKILL.md, revision of 3 September 2026). anthropics/skills repository.

entries.caveats: The balance point differs by audience: experts and design-interested people accept more novelty. The MAYA phrase is the industrial designer Raymond Loewy's maxim, not the evidence.
entries.sleekRelevance: The most direct evidence-based recipe for 'sophisticated, not generic': a typical frame plus one advanced element.

entries.principle: Generous space signals prestige, within limits
entries.claim: Space around a product or message raises perceived prestige and quality in the contexts studied. The meaning comes from cultural history, not from the eye, and too much space on a task page lowers perceived usability.
entries.mechanism: In Western commercial design, empty space became associated with upmarket brands. In stores, more space per product makes each item look more valuable. People read the cue because they have learned it, so it varies between cultures.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — separation makes groups easier to see, until content is pushed out of view
effects.satisfaction: raises — higher prestige and aesthetic ratings in the studies
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — clearer grouping helps; extra scrolling and hidden content hurt

designMoves: Give the main message and the key product or figure clear space on all sides; reduce competing items instead of shrinking margins.
Use larger gaps between groups than within groups so space carries structure.
On task and commerce pages, keep working content dominant: in the one web experiment, usability ratings fell when white space exceeded about half of the page.
On phones, keep the space between groups and trim the outer margins.
antiPatterns: Filling every gap with a badge, a banner or secondary content.
A vast empty hero that pushes all content below the fold.
Equal spacing everywhere, so that space carries no meaning.

howToCheck.machine: Compute the share of the first viewport that is background. Compare gap sizes within and between groups. Flag pages at either extreme of content density.
howToCheck.human: Does the page look confident or empty? Can the main task start without scrolling?

evidence.strengthNote: Pracejus, Olsen and O'Guinn (2006): studies of print advertising showing that white space conveys prestige-related brand meanings, grounded in a historical analysis; their 2013 paper found that the meanings differ across cultures. Sevilla and Townsend (2016): lab and field studies; more space between products raised aesthetic appeal, store prestige and purchase. Coursaris and Kripintris (2012): one between-subjects experiment with 25%, 50% and 75% white space on an e-commerce site; perceived usability dropped above 50%. The advertising and retail results transfer to interfaces by analogy; only the last study used a website.

sources.citation: Pracejus, J. W., Olsen, G. D., & O'Guinn, T. C. (2006). How nothing became something: White space, rhetoric, history, and meaning. Journal of Consumer Research, 33(1), 82-90.

Pracejus, J. W., O'Guinn, T. C., & Olsen, G. D. (2013). When white space is more than 'burning money': Economic signaling meets visual commercial rhetoric. International Journal of Research in Marketing, 30(3), 211-218.

Sevilla, J., & Townsend, C. (2016). The space-to-product ratio effect: How interstitial space influences product aesthetic appeal, store perceptions, and product preference. Journal of Marketing Research, 53(5), 665-681.
Coursaris, C. K., & Kripintris, K. (2012). Web aesthetics and usability: An empirical study of the effects of white space. International Journal of E-Business Research, 8(1), 35-53.

entries.caveats: The cue depends on culture. It has not been tested on dense operational apps, where users value information per screen. The 50% figure comes from a single study of one shop design. The title of the 2013 paper is recalled; its journal, volume and pages were confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Space is the best-evidenced premium cue available, and it costs nothing. It works as a signal only when it is clearly deliberate and structured.

entries.principle: Visually simple designs are liked, but can be valued lower
entries.claim: People believe that visually simpler designs cost less to produce. In side-by-side comparisons they are willing to pay less for the simpler version, even when they like both versions equally.
entries.mechanism: A lay belief links visual detail to time and effort, and effort to cost. The belief shows when versions are compared directly. It weakens when a design is judged alone or when people learn that both versions took similar effort.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the effect concerns judgments of value
effects.satisfaction: mixed — liking stays the same; perceived worth can drop
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not tested in the cited experiments

designMoves: In a minimal design, show evidence of care where a viewer can see it: precise typography, considered detail in key components, high-quality imagery, specific content.
Where price or value is judged next to alternatives, avoid looking like the bare version.
State effort or process where it is true and relevant (how something is made, checked or sourced).
antiPatterns: Minimalism that is only absence: default type, default spacing, no detail.
A pricing or product page that looks like an unstyled template next to richer competitors.

howToCheck.human: Show the page beside two competitors. Ask which looks most expensive to make, and why.

evidence.strengthNote: Min, Liu and Anderson (2025; online in 2024), Journal of Consumer Research: several experiments with product designs. Only the abstract was available in this session; sample sizes were not checked. The stimuli were products, not interfaces. A 2025 package-design paper reports that visual complexity can shift preference in either direction, depending on what consumers weigh.

sources.citation: Min, L., Liu, P. J., & Anderson, C. L. (2025). The visual complexity = higher production cost lay belief. Journal of Consumer Research, 51(6), 1167-1185.

entries.caveats: This sits beside the first-impression research without contradicting it: low complexity is liked more at a glance, and it can still be valued less in a direct comparison. The effect weakens when a design is evaluated alone, which is how most pages are seen.
entries.sleekRelevance: Explains why sparse template output looks cheap while sparse luxury design does not: the latter carries visible precision. Restraint needs visible craft to read as premium.

entries.principle: Perceived craftsmanship is a measurable part of visual appeal
entries.claim: People's ratings of website aesthetics separate into four related facets: simplicity, diversity, colorfulness and craftsmanship (whether the design looks skillfully and carefully made with current means).
entries.mechanism: Viewers notice coherence and care, or their absence, as a distinct quality: whether elements fit together and whether the design looks up to date and professionally executed.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — simplicity and coherent execution ease parsing
effects.satisfaction: raises — each facet contributes to overall appeal
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — simplicity ratings track clarity and order

designMoves: Review the four facets separately: is the page orderly (simplicity), visually interesting (diversity), well colored (colorfulness) and deliberately finished (craftsmanship)?
Remove visible execution flaws: misaligned edges, inconsistent radii and shadows, mixed icon styles, stretched or blurry images, uneven spacing.
Use current rendering capabilities properly: sharp images on high-density screens, well-loaded fonts.
antiPatterns: Mixed icon families and stroke weights.
Inconsistent corner radii and shadow styles.
Images at the wrong resolution or aspect ratio.

howToCheck.machine: Detect inconsistent radii, shadow definitions, icon stroke widths and off-grid alignments. Compare each image's natural size with its rendered size and the device pixel ratio.
howToCheck.human: Rate the page with the four-facet questionnaire (VisAWI) or its short form, and compare with a reference site.

evidence.strengthNote: Moshagen and Thielsch (2010): seven studies that developed and validated the Visual Aesthetics of Websites Inventory (VisAWI); four facets with good reliability and validity; a short form followed in 2013. This is a questionnaire-development paper: it shows what people perceive, not which design changes cause the perception.

sources.citation: Moshagen, M., & Thielsch, M. T. (2010). Facets of visual aesthetics. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 68(10), 689-709.
Moshagen, M., & Thielsch, M. T. (2013). A short version of the visual aesthetics of websites inventory. Behaviour & Information Technology, 32(12), 1305-1311.

entries.caveats: The facets correlate with each other. Which concrete details drive the craftsmanship rating has not been isolated by experiment; the detail lists that designers use are informed opinion (see invisible-details-craft-layer).
entries.sleekRelevance: Gives 'looks well made' a research-backed definition and a questionnaire. It is the nearest measured construct to 'premium'.

entries.principle: People value what visibly took effort
entries.claim: People rate the same work as better and worth more when they believe more effort went into it, and they value a service more when they can see it working on their behalf.
entries.mechanism: Quality is hard to judge directly, so people use effort as a shortcut (the effort heuristic). Showing the work a system is doing (operational transparency) triggers the same inference. The 'labor illusion' is the finding that the appearance of effort is enough to raise perceived value.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — it changes valuation, not effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — with visible, credible effort; lowers if the wait feels padded
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; the effect concerns value, not ease

designMoves: During a necessary wait, say what the system is doing in specific terms instead of showing a bare spinner.
For results from an AI model or a search, show the steps or sources behind the answer.
Show real evidence of care in the product: specific copy, considered details, finished empty and error states.
Keep the display honest: describe only work that is really happening.
antiPatterns: Artificial delays or invented progress steps.
A bare spinner for a long, multi-step operation.
Generated output with no visible reasoning or sources.

howToCheck.machine: For operations longer than a set time, verify that the loading state contains changing, descriptive text or step indicators and not only an indeterminate spinner.
howToCheck.human: Do the described steps match what the system does? Would a user feel misled on seeing the real process?

evidence.strengthNote: Kruger, Wirtz, Van Boven and Altermatt (2004): experiments in which poems, paintings and other items were rated higher when said to have taken longer to make. Buell and Norton (2011): five experiments that simulated online travel and dating searches; showing the work raised perceived value. Details beyond the abstracts were not re-checked in this session.

sources.citation: Kruger, J., Wirtz, D., Van Boven, L., & Altermatt, T. W. (2004). The effort heuristic. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 40(1), 91-98.
Buell, R. W., & Norton, M. I. (2011). The labor illusion: How operational transparency increases perceived value. Management Science, 57(9), 1564-1579.

entries.caveats: The effect depends on a good outcome; visible effort followed by a poor result backfires. Faking effort is deception (see deceptive-patterns-work-then-backfire). The finding is no license to slow a product down.
entries.sleekRelevance: Premium products make their care visible. In AI products especially, legible work is a quality cue that plain speed does not give.

entries.principle: Fast, steady response is read as quality
entries.claim: Interfaces that respond at once to input and do not shift under the user feel solid and well made. Popular statistics that tie a specific loading time to a specific share of lost visitors are vendor correlations, not laws.
entries.mechanism: Delay breaks the feeling of directly causing an effect: within about a tenth of a second a response is perceived as part of the action, and beyond about a second the user notices waiting. Unexpected movement makes the hand miss its target and the user distrust the page.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no need to hold the goal in mind through a wait
effects.satisfaction: raises — slow or unstable pages draw complaints and abandonment (the perception-cognition part holds the latency evidence)
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — an immediate response confirms that the action was right

designMoves: Acknowledge every input visibly at once (pressed state, focus ring, optimistic change), before the server answers.

Meet the 'good' bars of Google's Core Web Vitals: Interaction to Next Paint (the delay from an input to the next screen update) at or under 200 ms, Largest Contentful Paint (when the main content appears) at or under 2.5 s, Cumulative Layout Shift (unexpected movement) at or under 0.1.
Reserve space for images, fonts and late content so nothing jumps.
Never block the whole screen for a background save.
antiPatterns: Buttons with no pressed or loading state.
Layout that jumps as images or fonts arrive.
Quoting '53% of visitors leave after 3 seconds' as a universal threshold.

howToCheck.machine: Measure INP, LCP and CLS with the web-vitals library or Lighthouse on the rendered page; assert the thresholds 200 ms, 2.5 s and 0.1.
howToCheck.human: Use the page on a mid-range phone on a slow connection. Note every moment of doubt about whether a tap registered.

evidence.strengthNote: The response-time limits of about 0.1, 1 and 10 seconds are Nielsen's (1993) summary of older human-factors work; they are long-standing rules of thumb, and the perception-cognition part of this knowledge base treats them in detail ('response-time-limits', 'inp-responsiveness', 'latency-costs-gradual'). The Core Web Vitals thresholds are a vendor convention, read here from the web-vitals library documentation. The '53% abandon after 3 seconds' figure comes from Google's 2016 analysis of an opt-in sample of about 3,700 mobile sites; it is observational and was published by a company that sells advertising. No study was found that measures responsiveness against perceived premium quality directly.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (2010). Website response times. Nielsen Norman Group.
Google Chrome team. web-vitals library, README (rating thresholds for CLS, INP and LCP).
Google / DoubleClick (2016). The need for mobile speed.

entries.caveats: Raw speed is not the same as perceived speed; feedback and predictability matter as well (see waiting-feedback-and-certainty). The link from responsiveness to a premium impression is practitioner consensus plus inference.
entries.sleekRelevance: No visual treatment survives lag. Immediate, steady response is the behavioral half of 'sleek'.

entries.principle: Motion should explain a change, be brief, and be optional
entries.claim: Short transitions can help people follow what changed on screen, and design systems keep interface motion between roughly 70 and 700 ms, mostly at the short end. The belief that smooth motion makes a product feel premium is practitioner consensus, not a tested finding.
entries.mechanism: An abrupt change forces people to work out what happened; a brief transition shows where something came from or went. Long or frequent motion delays the user and pulls attention away from content.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — lowers it when motion shows cause and effect; raises it when motion is decorative or slow
effects.satisfaction: mixed — pleasant in small doses, irritating when repeated or slow
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when motion connects an action to its result

designMoves: Animate only to show cause and effect or a change of state.

Use short durations. One widely used system (IBM Carbon) specifies 70 and 110 ms for small interactions such as buttons and fades, 150 and 240 ms for small expansions and notifications, 400 ms for large expansions and 700 ms for background dimming.
Animate transform and opacity; avoid animating layout properties such as width, height, top and left.
Make animations interruptible by user input.
Honor the reduce-motion preference with a reduced variant (see reduced-motion-floor).
Reserve expressive, highly visible motion for occasional important moments.
antiPatterns: Entrance effects triggered by scrolling on every section.
Transitions longer than the action deserves.
Motion that cannot be turned off.
The CSS declaration 'transition: all'.

howToCheck.machine: Parse computed transition and animation durations and properties. Flag durations above a ceiling, animated layout properties, 'transition: all' and missing handling of prefers-reduced-motion. Record a performance trace to check for dropped frames.
howToCheck.human: Use the main flow ten times in a row. Note any animation that starts to feel slow.

evidence.strengthNote: The duration values are from IBM's Carbon design system and the rules on what to animate are from Vercel's published interface guidelines; both were read in this session and both are vendor guidance. Peer-reviewed support that animated transitions help people track change (Heer and Robertson, 2007) and the caution that animation often fails to beat static displays (Tversky, Morrison and Bétrancourt, 2002) are cited from memory and were not re-checked. No controlled study was found that links motion smoothness to perceived premium quality.

sources.citation: IBM. Carbon Design System, Motion overview (duration tokens; productive and expressive motion). carbon-design-system/carbon-website repository.
Vercel. Web Interface Guidelines. vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines repository.
Heer, J., & Robertson, G. (2007). Animated transitions in statistical data graphics. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, 13(6), 1240-1247.
Tversky, B., Morrison, J. B., & Bétrancourt, M. (2002). Animation: Can it facilitate? International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 57(4), 247-262.

entries.caveats: Motion can cause dizziness and nausea for people with vestibular disorders. The numbers differ between design systems; they are conventions, not thresholds from research.
entries.sleekRelevance: Practitioners agree that restrained, fast, physically plausible motion separates polished products from generated ones. Treat it as a craft convention and keep it subordinate to responsiveness.

entries.principle: Typographic quality changes mood and the impression a brand gives
entries.claim: In one study, well-set text put readers in a better mood and made time seem to pass faster, without changing reading speed or comprehension. Typeface design also shifts the impressions people form of the sender.
entries.mechanism: Good typography removes small frictions that readers do not consciously notice; the saved effort shows up as mood. Features of letterforms (harmony, elaborateness, weight, naturalness) carry associations that people transfer to the sender.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — slightly, below awareness
effects.satisfaction: raises — better mood during reading
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Choose the typeface deliberately for the impression wanted; do not accept a tool's default family without a reason.
Set a clear scale with few sizes and weights, and use it consistently.
Apply fine typographic refinements where the font supports them: proper kerning, ligatures, real small caps, correct quotation marks and dashes.
Use tabular (equal-width) numerals where numbers are compared in columns.
antiPatterns: Default system or template fonts used without a decision.
Synthesized bold or italic, or stretched type.
Straight quotes, and hyphens used as dashes, in finished copy.
Proportional numerals in tables of figures.

howToCheck.machine: List the font families, sizes and weights in use; flag more than a set number. Check font-variant-numeric on tabular data. Detect straight quotes in body copy and synthesized bold or italic.
howToCheck.human: Read a full screen of real content. Does anything catch the eye for the wrong reason?

evidence.strengthNote: Larson and Picard (2005): two small studies compared a well-typeset and a poorly typeset version of the same reading material; no difference in speed or comprehension, but better results on mood-sensitive measures (estimates of elapsed time and certain cognitive tasks). Sample sizes were not confirmed in this session; one author worked at Microsoft, which develops reading and font technology, and no independent replication is known. Henderson, Giese and Cote (2004) on typeface impressions is cited from memory and was not re-checked.

sources.citation: Larson, K., & Picard, R. W. (2005). The aesthetics of reading. Human-Computer Interaction Consortium Conference (MIT Media Lab publication).
Henderson, P. W., Giese, J. L., & Cote, J. A. (2004). Impression management using typeface design. Journal of Marketing, 68(4), 60-72.

entries.caveats: A small, old, unreplicated mood study: treat the direction as plausible and the size as unknown. The perception-cognition part covers legibility evidence.
entries.sleekRelevance: Practitioners locate most of the difference between generic and refined in typography. The evidence supports an effect on mood and impression, and it is thin on which details matter most.

entries.principle: Small unrequested details add up to a 'finished' feel
entries.claim: Experienced interface designers hold that a product feels premium when many small details are right: number alignment, text wrapping, loading-state timing, focus behavior, preserved state. This is expert consensus; the individual details have not been tested for their effect on perceived quality.
entries.mechanism: Each flaw is a small interruption or a sign of inattention. Viewers rarely name the details, but they notice the sum as care or carelessness (craftsmanship-facet and visible-effort-raises-value give the supported general mechanisms).

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer small interruptions
effects.satisfaction: raises — according to practitioner experience; unmeasured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — state is preserved and feedback is steady

designMoves: Delay spinners and skeletons by about 150 to 300 ms, and keep them visible for at least about 300 to 500 ms once shown, to avoid flicker.
Use tabular numerals for figures that are compared.
Use the single ellipsis character and curly quotation marks; keep units attached to numbers with non-breaking spaces.
Keep state in the URL so that back, forward, refresh and sharing work.
Reserve space for images and late content so nothing shifts; make skeleton placeholders match the final layout.
Confirm destructive actions or offer undo; warn before navigation that would lose unsaved input.
antiPatterns: A spinner that flashes on fast responses.
Lost scroll position or filters after going back.
Numbers that jiggle as they update.
Layout jumps when images load.

howToCheck.machine: Script checks: the URL changes when filters or tabs change; back restores scroll position; images declare width and height; numeric columns use tabular numerals; loading indicators respect the minimum delay; layout shift stays under the threshold.
howToCheck.human: Use the product for ten minutes looking only for small annoyances. List them.

evidence.strengthNote: The rules and numbers come from Vercel's published web interface guidelines, read in this session. They are one company's practice. No controlled evidence isolates these details; the general link between perceived care and perceived quality has peer-reviewed support (Moshagen and Thielsch, 2010; Kruger et al., 2004).

sources.citation: Vercel. Web Interface Guidelines. vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines repository.
Moshagen, M., & Thielsch, M. T. (2010). Facets of visual aesthetics. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 68(10), 689-709.

entries.caveats: Lists of such details reflect current taste and platform capabilities and will change. Several items overlap with accessibility and performance requirements that rest on firmer ground.
entries.sleekRelevance: This is the layer most often missing from machine-generated interfaces and most often present in admired ones. It is cheap to specify in a build prompt and easy to verify.

entries.principle: Folklore: 'dark mode looks more premium'
entries.claim: No peer-reviewed study was found that tests whether a dark interface theme is perceived as more premium. Related research finds that dark and black-and-white treatments raise the perceived luxury of logos and of luxury advertisements, and that light themes read better for most people with normal vision.
entries.mechanism: Darkness and black are associated with luxury and formality in several consumer contexts, so the belief is plausible for brand surfaces. Reading follows different rules: dark text on a light background is easier for most eyes.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — a dark theme can raise reading effort for long text and reduce glare in dim rooms
effects.satisfaction: mixed — many users hold a firm preference for one theme or the other
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; a theme does not change how things work

designMoves: Choose the default theme for the content and the setting (long reading and data entry favor light; media viewing and dim environments favor dark), not for a premium claim.
If both themes are offered, design both to the same standard and follow the system preference.
In a dark theme, check contrast for every text and control state.
antiPatterns: A dark theme chosen only to look expensive, with low-contrast gray text.
A dark theme that is an automatic inversion of the light one.

howToCheck.machine: Compute contrast ratios for all text and control states in each theme. If two themes exist, verify that the page responds to prefers-color-scheme.
howToCheck.human: Read a long passage in each theme, in a bright room and in a dim one.

evidence.strengthNote: No direct evidence for the interface claim was found in this session (the search covered 2022 to 2026). Adjacent peer-reviewed findings: black-and-white design raised evaluations of luxury brand advertisements through perceived luxuriousness, and darker logos were seen as more luxurious (Smale et al., 2025). NN/g's 2020 review of the academic literature concluded that light mode gives better reading performance for people with normal vision and that some people with certain visual impairments do better in dark mode; NN/g ran no study of its own. All three are known here through search results.

sources.citation: Smale et al. (2025). Darker logos are seen as for-profits and lighter logos as nonprofits. Psychology & Marketing.
[Authors not confirmed] (2022). What is the glamor of black-and-white? The effect of color design on evaluations of luxury brand ads.
Budiu, R. (2020). Dark mode vs. light mode: Which is better? Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: the luxury association may transfer to interfaces. It is untested.
entries.sleekRelevance: Dark themes are common among admired developer tools, which is a genre convention worth knowing. It is not proof that dark equals premium.

entries.principle: People judge credibility first by how a site looks
entries.claim: When ordinary people explain why they find a website credible or not, they mention its overall visual design more often than anything else.
entries.mechanism: Prominence-interpretation theory: people can only judge what they notice, and the look is noticed first and by everyone, while checking sources or credentials takes effort. A well-made site also works as a costly signal: a firm that visibly invested in its site is assumed to be capable.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the judgment is made without analysis
effects.satisfaction: raises — trust is a precondition for continuing
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — clear information structure was the second most cited factor

designMoves: Make layout, typography, imagery and color scheme look deliberate and consistent on every page where a newcomer may land.
Organize information so its structure is visible; structure was the second most cited credibility factor.
Show that a real organization stands behind the site: name, address, contact route, people.
Keep the look appropriate to the field; a design can be attractive and still wrong for a bank or a clinic.
antiPatterns: A polished home page with neglected inner pages.
A look that contradicts the seriousness of the subject.
No identifiable organization or contact route.

howToCheck.machine: Verify the presence of an organization name, contact details and an about or imprint link on every page. Check that type and color tokens are consistent across pages.
howToCheck.human: Ask a newcomer: would you give this site your email address or card number? Why?

evidence.strengthNote: Fogg et al. (2002 report; 2003 conference paper): 2,684 participants each evaluated two live sites and left comments; 46.1% of the comments mentioned design look and 28.5% information design or structure. This is a large comment-coding study, not a controlled experiment, and the data are from 2002. A companion study found that domain experts weighed content and source more than consumers did (recalled, not re-checked). Schlosser, White and Lloyd (2006) reported experiments in which perceived investment in site design raised belief in the firm's ability and raised purchase intentions; only the citation was confirmed in this session, and the finding is stated from memory.

sources.citation: Fogg, B. J., Soohoo, C., Danielson, D. R., Marable, L., Stanford, J., & Tauber, E. R. (2003). How do users evaluate the credibility of Web sites? A study with over 2,500 participants. Proceedings of DUX 2003.
Nielsen Norman Group. Prominence-interpretation theory (article on Fogg's theory).

Schlosser, A. E., White, T. B., & Lloyd, S. M. (2006). Converting web site visitors into buyers: How web site investment increases consumer trusting beliefs and online purchase intentions. Journal of Marketing, 70(2), 133-148.

entries.caveats: Comments reveal what people notice and say, not necessarily what drives behavior. Looking credible and being credible are different things; a polished look also helps fraudulent sites. The title of the 2003 conference paper is recalled; the figures were confirmed through reports of the 2002 study.
entries.sleekRelevance: A refined, coherent look is not vanity. For newcomers it is the main evidence that the organization is competent.

entries.principle: Small flaws cost trust
entries.claim: Typographical errors, broken links, poor style and incomplete pages lower perceived site quality, and through it trust and the intention to buy. What counts is whether the flaw is noticed.
entries.mechanism: People treat a visible mistake as a sample of the organization's care: if they missed this, what else did they miss? The first noticed flaw changes the overall judgment; each further flaw adds less.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — errors interrupt reading and tasks
effects.satisfaction: lowers — perceived quality and trust drop
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — broken links and missing content break expectations

designMoves: Proofread all visible text, including error messages, empty states, alternative text and legal pages.
Check every link and image on the built site; release no placeholder text or images.
Keep content complete and dated; finish or remove 'coming soon' sections.
Keep the site up: failed loads count as flaws.
antiPatterns: Lorem ipsum or placeholder images in production.
Dead links from the main navigation.
Spelling mistakes in headings or buttons.
Out-of-date copyright years and notices.

howToCheck.machine: Crawl for broken links and missing images. Spell-check the rendered text. Search for placeholder strings (lorem, TODO, example.com). Check for console errors.
howToCheck.human: Read every screen aloud once.

evidence.strengthNote: Everard and Galletta (2005): experiment with 272 student volunteers on an online store; errors, poor style and incompleteness each lowered perceived quality, which predicted trust and purchase intention; the perception of flaws mattered more than the actual flaws, and each further flaw had a smaller effect. Fogg et al. (2001): online survey with 51 items completed by 1,441 people on what makes sites credible. Stanford's credibility guidelines (2002) advise avoiding errors of all types, however small. Student sample; the studies are about two decades old.

sources.citation: Everard, A., & Galletta, D. F. (2005). How presentation flaws affect perceived site quality, trust, and intention to purchase from an online store. Journal of Management Information Systems, 22(3), 55-95.
Fogg, B. J., Marshall, J., Laraki, O., et al. (2001). What makes Web sites credible? A report on a large quantitative study. Proceedings of CHI 2001, 61-68.
Fogg, B. J. (2002). Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility. Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab.

entries.caveats: The size of the effect in today's market, where users meet many flawed sites, is not known. Generated text and images add new kinds of flaw (plausible but wrong details) that these studies did not cover.
entries.sleekRelevance: Polish is partly the absence of small errors. One typo in a hero heading undoes a great deal of visual work.

entries.principle: Real, informative images are looked at; generic ones are ignored
entries.claim: In eyetracking research, people look at images that carry information relevant to their task (products, real staff) and skip decorative filler such as stock photos of generic people.
entries.mechanism: People scan for information. An image that answers a question earns attention; an image recognized as decoration is filtered out like an advertisement. Specific images also serve as evidence that the organization and its product are real.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer elements to skip past once filler is removed
effects.satisfaction: raises — content answers questions
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; the finding concerns attention and trust

designMoves: Use photographs of the real product, place, team or work.
Remove images that carry no information; let type and space do the job.
Caption images so their relevance is clear.
If illustration is used, make it specific to the subject.
antiPatterns: Stock photos of smiling models, headsets or handshakes.
A decorative hero image unrelated to the offering.
Generated images with visible artifacts.

howToCheck.machine: List images that lack informative alternative text or captions. Flag images served from known stock-photo hosts. Flag decorative images that take more than a set share of the first viewport.
howToCheck.human: For each image ask: what would be lost if it were removed?

evidence.strengthNote: NN/g eyetracking research reported by Nielsen (2010); sample details were not available in this session. The NN/g finding concerns attention. The link to trust rests on the Stanford credibility guidance (show that a real organization stands behind the site) and is otherwise an inference.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (2010). Photos as web content. Nielsen Norman Group.
Fogg, B. J. (2002). Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility. Stanford Persuasive Technology Lab.

entries.caveats: A stock image that carries real information can work. Photos of people help more in some cultures and contexts than in others.
entries.sleekRelevance: Subject-specific imagery is one of the few levers that makes a page impossible to mistake for a template.

entries.principle: Disclose costs, terms and identity before people commit
entries.claim: Sites earn trust by stating prices, fees, terms and who they are up front. Unexpected extra costs are the most reported reason for abandoning an online purchase, and a noticeable share of shoppers abandon because they do not trust the site with card details.
entries.mechanism: A surprise late in a process is experienced as a broken promise and makes people re-examine everything before it. Disclosure up front removes the risk people are trying to assess. Visible care around sensitive fields answers the security question at the moment it arises.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no need to hunt for the catch
effects.satisfaction: raises — fewer unpleasant surprises
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the process behaves as predicted

designMoves: Show the full price, including shipping, taxes and fees, as early as it can be computed.
State subscription, renewal and cancellation terms next to the commit button.
Provide contact details and an identifiable organization on every page.
Set the payment or sensitive-data area visually apart (a bordered or tinted panel with a short reassurance) so that it looks deliberately secured.
Keep content current and link to independent sources or reviews.
antiPatterns: Fees revealed at the last step.
Pre-ticked add-ons.
Contact details hidden or absent.
A payment form that looks less finished than the rest of the site.

howToCheck.machine: In a scripted checkout, compare the first displayed price with the final total. Flag pre-checked optional boxes. Verify contact and terms links near commit controls.
howToCheck.human: Walk through purchase or sign-up. Note every piece of information that arrives later than it was wanted.

evidence.strengthNote: NN/g named four trust factors in 1999 (design quality, up-front disclosure, comprehensive and current content, connection to the rest of the web) and reports that a 2016 round of research confirmed them. Baymard Institute surveys of US adults: extra costs lead the reasons for abandonment (reported as 39% to 48% across survey years and bases), and about 18% to 21% cite distrust with card information; Baymard's qualitative testing found that visually reinforced payment fields raise perceived security. The percentages are from secondary summaries of Baymard pages and vary by year. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility recommends stating fees at the start of a task.

sources.citation: Nielsen Norman Group. Trustworthiness in web design: 4 credibility factors.
Baymard Institute. Cart abandonment rate statistics (reasons for abandonment survey).
Baymard Institute. How users perceive security during the checkout flow (perceived security of payment form).

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (pattern: notify users of fees and charges at the start of a task). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: Self-reported reasons for abandonment are not proof of behavior. Perceived security is not real security; visual reassurance must not stand in for the real thing.
entries.sleekRelevance: Confident products state their terms plainly. Evasive pricing is the fastest way for a beautiful page to feel like a trap.

entries.principle: Folklore: '94% of first impressions are design-related' and '75% judge credibility by design'
entries.claim: Neither figure is a general fact: the 94% comes from a study of 15 women evaluating health websites, where it described reasons for rejecting sites. The 75% has no traceable primary source; the Stanford study it is attributed to reported 46.1%.
entries.mechanism: Statistics lose their context as marketing articles copy them from each other; a narrow finding becomes a universal rule.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the entry concerns a claim, not a design
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the cited studies did not measure satisfaction
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured
