designMoves: Cite the supported version: in a large 2002 study, 46.1% of credibility comments mentioned visual design, more than any other factor.
Use the health-site finding as it was reported: poor design led to early rejection, and content quality and personal relevance led to selection and trust.
Keep both percentages out of briefs and pitches.
antiPatterns: Quoting 94% or 75% as universal.
Concluding that content matters little.

howToCheck.human: Trace any statistic in a design rationale to a primary source before relying on it.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the popular claims. Sillence, Briggs, Fishwick and Harris (2004): fifteen women facing a health decision searched for advice over four weeks; design appeal predicted rejection, and credibility and personalization of content predicted selection. The 94% figure appears in secondary summaries and was not checked against the paper's text. No primary source for 75% was found; several sites attribute it to Stanford's credibility project, whose own large study reported 46.1%.

sources.citation: Sillence, E., Briggs, P., Fishwick, L., & Harris, P. (2004). Trust and mistrust of online health sites. Proceedings of CHI 2004, 663-670.
ClickZ (2002). Study: For site cred, looks matter (news report of the Stanford and Consumer WebWatch study).

entries.caveats: The underlying direction is real: design acts as an early filter. The numbers are the problem.
entries.sleekRelevance: Protects the case for good design from resting on numbers that collapse under one question.

entries.principle: Norman's three levels: visceral, behavioral, reflective
entries.claim: Norman's framework describes three levels at which a product affects people: visceral (the immediate reaction to how it looks and feels), behavioral (the experience of using it) and reflective (what it means to the person and says about them). It is a useful vocabulary, not a tested law.
entries.mechanism: The levels correspond to kinds of processing: fast, automatic reactions to appearance; learned, largely subconscious skill in use; slow, conscious interpretation and memory. Reflection can excuse faults at the other levels, or condemn a product that works.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — a framework, not an intervention
effects.satisfaction: mixed — satisfaction can arise or fail at each level
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when the behavioral level is right

designMoves: Review a design at each level separately: the first look, the use, and the story the user would tell about it.
Do not let one level stand in for another: a striking look does not supply good behavior.
For the reflective level, make the product's purpose and values specific in copy and detail.
antiPatterns: Treating emotional design as decoration or mascots.
Optimizing the first look only.

howToCheck.human: Three questions after a session: What did you think at first sight? How did using it go? How would you describe it to a friend?

evidence.strengthNote: Norman (2004) is a scholarly book that synthesizes emotion research into a design framework. The three-level division has not been validated as a model. Related claims, such as 'attractive things work better', have mixed experimental support (see aesthetics-performance-small-effect). Known here through secondary descriptions of the book.

sources.citation: Norman, D. A. (2004). Emotional Design: Why We Love (or Hate) Everyday Things. Basic Books.

entries.caveats: The levels interact and are hard to separate in practice.
entries.sleekRelevance: Sophistication is largely reflective: it lies in what the product's choices say about its makers and its user.

entries.principle: People judge products on two dimensions: getting things done, and how it feels to own and use them
entries.claim: People perceive pragmatic quality (useful and usable for tasks) and hedonic quality (stimulating, and expressing identity) as separate. Beauty ratings follow hedonic quality and stay stable; judgments of usability and overall goodness change with experience.
entries.mechanism: Pragmatic qualities serve 'do-goals' (finish the task). Hedonic qualities serve 'be-goals' (feel competent, be a person of taste). Both feed the overall verdict.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the model describes perception
effects.satisfaction: raises — both dimensions contribute; hedonic quality matters most for attachment
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — through the pragmatic dimension only

designMoves: Evaluate both dimensions; a tool can be efficient and still leave people cold.
Decide what the product should let the user feel or express (careful, creative, expert) and reflect that in look and wording.
Measure both with a questionnaire that separates them (for example the UEQ; see standard-questionnaires-sus-ueq).
antiPatterns: Treating a product that passes usability tests as finished.
Adding stimulation that obstructs tasks.

howToCheck.human: Run the UEQ after a task session and compare the pragmatic and hedonic scale scores.

evidence.strengthNote: Hassenzahl (2004): a study of four skins for an MP3 player; beauty related mainly to the hedonic attribute 'identification', and experience changed ratings of usability and goodness but not of beauty. A small study with one product type; the two-dimension model has since been used widely and underlies the UEQ. Details are from secondary summaries.

sources.citation: Hassenzahl, M. (2004). The interplay of beauty, goodness, and usability in interactive products. Human-Computer Interaction, 19(4), 319-349.
Karapanos, E., Zimmerman, J., Forlizzi, J., & Martens, J.-B. (2009). User experience over time: An initial framework. Proceedings of CHI 2009, 729-738.

entries.caveats: The two dimensions correlate (halo effects). Which matters more depends on the situation: under time pressure, pragmatic quality dominates.
entries.sleekRelevance: 'Modern, sleek, sophisticated' is a hedonic goal. It needs its own decisions and its own measurement, alongside usability.

entries.principle: Memory of an experience is dominated by its most intense moment and its end
entries.claim: People's later ratings of an experience are predicted well by its peak and its final moments, and its length matters little. In interface studies the effect is weaker and less reliable.
entries.mechanism: Memory does not store an average of every moment. It keeps a few representative moments, especially the most intense and the last, and people consult that memory when they rate the experience or choose again.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the rule concerns memory
effects.satisfaction: raises — if the worst moment is softened and the ending is good
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; the rule concerns memory, not ease

designMoves: Find the worst moment of each main flow (often an error, a wait or a payment step) and reduce it first.
Design the end of each flow: a clear confirmation, the result shown, a sensible next step.
Do not end on a chore (a survey, an upsell or a sign-up wall) after the task is complete.
Put a necessary hard step early or in the middle, not last.
antiPatterns: A success page that is an advertisement.
Onboarding that ends on a permissions prompt.
The most error-prone step placed last.

howToCheck.machine: Verify that each completing action leads to a distinct success state with a result and a next step. Flag flows whose final screen contains a form or modal unrelated to the task.
howToCheck.human: Ask users after a session which moment they remember. Check what the last screen was.

evidence.strengthNote: Alaybek et al. (2022) pooled 174 effect sizes: the peak-end composite correlated r = .58 with retrospective evaluations, robustly across conditions, and predicted about as well as the overall average. Classic demonstration: Kahneman et al. (1993), cold-water trials in which a majority of participants chose to repeat the longer trial that ended less painfully. In human-computer interaction, Cockburn, Quinn and Gutwin (2015) observed the predicted preference in only one of three form-filling conditions, and later work reports mixed results.

sources.citation: Alaybek, B., Dalal, R. S., Fyffe, S., et al. (2022). All's well that ends (and peaks) well? A meta-analysis of the peak-end rule and duration neglect. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 170, 104149.
Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401-405.
Cockburn, A., Quinn, P., & Gutwin, C. (2015). Examining the peak-end effects of subjective experience. Proceedings of CHI 2015, 357-366.

entries.caveats: The average of the experience predicts memory about as well, so the rule is no license to neglect the middle. The evidence for interfaces specifically is mixed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Refined products finish well: confirmations, receipts and completion states get as much care as the hero.

entries.principle: People speed up near a goal, and a head start increases persistence
entries.claim: Effort increases as people approach a goal (the goal-gradient effect), and people given a head start toward a goal are more likely to complete it (the endowed progress effect).
entries.mechanism: As the goal nears, each remaining step is a larger share of what is left, so it feels more valuable. A head start reframes the task as already under way, and people dislike abandoning progress.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — a visible structure shows what remains
effects.satisfaction: raises — visible progress is rewarding
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — people know where they are in a process

designMoves: Show progress in multi-step tasks, with the number of steps known from the start.
Count real completed work as progress (information already known, steps done at sign-up).
Break long tasks into stages with their own completion points.
Keep progress indicators truthful; do not invent steps to show early progress.
antiPatterns: Multi-step flows with no indication of length.
Progress bars that stall or reset.
Pre-filled progress that corresponds to no real work.

howToCheck.machine: In multi-step flows, verify that a step indicator exists, that the total stays the same across steps and that the indicated position matches the actual step.
howToCheck.human: Ask users in the middle of a flow how much they think remains.

evidence.strengthNote: Kivetz, Urminsky and Zheng (2006): field and lab studies, including a cafe loyalty card on which purchases accelerated toward the reward, and a 12-stamp card with two free stamps that customers completed faster than a 10-stamp card. Nunes and Drèze (2006): a car-wash field experiment with 300 customers in which the head-start card was redeemed at roughly double the rate (commonly cited as 34% versus 19%; these figures were not re-checked). Both are marketing studies of loyalty programs; transfer to interface flows is by analogy. No check for replications was possible in this session.

sources.citation: Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., & Zheng, Y. (2006). The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected: Purchase acceleration, illusionary goal progress, and customer retention. Journal of Marketing Research, 43(1), 39-58.
Nunes, J. C., & Drèze, X. (2006). The endowed progress effect: How artificial advancement increases effort. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(4), 504-512.

entries.caveats: The head start in the loyalty-card studies was illusory by design. In a product, artificial progress is a deceptive pattern. A progress indicator can also discourage when it reveals that a task is long.
entries.sleekRelevance: Well-made flows always tell users where they are. An honest, quiet progress indicator is part of a composed interface.

entries.principle: The Zeigarnik effect is weaker than its reputation
entries.claim: A 2025 meta-analysis found no general memory advantage for unfinished tasks (the Zeigarnik effect). It did find a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks (the Ovsiankina effect).
entries.mechanism: An unfinished task can leave a pull toward completing it. The pull shows in behavior: people go back to the task. It does not reliably show as better recall.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — no reliable effect is established; the claim that open tasks occupy the mind is unproven
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Do not justify incomplete-profile nags, streaks or cliffhangers by citing the Zeigarnik effect.
Use the supported part: make it easy to resume interrupted work (save state; show where the user left off).
If completion prompts are used, justify them by the user's benefit and test them.
antiPatterns: Tasks left open on purpose to create tension.
A persistent 'profile 80% complete' banner with no value to the user.

howToCheck.machine: Leave a flow midway and return: verify that state is restored and that a resume entry point is shown.
howToCheck.human: Review every completion prompt: does finishing help the user, or only the product's metrics?

evidence.strengthNote: Ghibellini and Meier (2025), Humanities and Social Sciences Communications: no memory advantage for unfinished tasks; a general tendency to resume them. Secondary sources give differing counts of included studies, which were not confirmed here. The abstract notes that the memory advantage has proven difficult to replicate. The grade applies to the corrected claim; the popular claim would be D.

sources.citation: Ghibellini, R., & Meier, B. (2025). Interruption, recall and resumption: A meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 12, 962.

entries.caveats: The meta-analysis covers laboratory tasks. The absence of a universal memory effect does not mean that nobody ever remembers an open task better.

entries.principle: Delight works only on top of things that work, and it fades into expectation
entries.claim: Surface delight (a charming animation, a witty line) has little effect unless the product is already functional, reliable and usable. Satisfaction comes from experience meeting or exceeding expectation, and yesterday's pleasant surprise becomes today's baseline.
entries.mechanism: People judge against what they expected. A flourish on a broken product draws attention to the breakage. As a feature becomes common, expectations rise, and what once delighted is merely required (in Kano's model, delighters decay into basics).

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — flourishes add load if they delay tasks
effects.satisfaction: mixed — raises when the basics are met; lowers when they are not, or when the flourish repeats
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; delight is not expected to make things easier

designMoves: Get function, reliability and usability right before adding flourishes.
Put small pleasures at natural pauses (completion, empty states), never in the path of a frequent action.
Make repeated flourishes short, varied or skippable.
Prefer deep delight: the task turning out easier or faster than expected.
antiPatterns: Confetti on routine actions.
Jokes in error messages when something has gone wrong.
An animated mascot on a slow page.

howToCheck.machine: Flag celebratory animations attached to high-frequency actions. Verify that flourishes respect reduced motion and do not delay the next interaction.
howToCheck.human: Use the feature twenty times. Is the flourish still welcome?

evidence.strengthNote: NN/g's theory of user delight (surface versus deep delight) is an expert framework built on its testing experience and on Walter's hierarchy of user needs. Expectation-confirmation theory (Oliver, 1980; Bhattacherjee, 2001) and Kano's model (1984) are established peer-reviewed frameworks, cited from memory and not re-checked here. Direct experiments on interface flourishes are scarce.

sources.citation: Fessenden, T. (2017). A theory of user delight: Why usability is the foundation for delightful experiences. Nielsen Norman Group.
Oliver, R. L. (1980). A cognitive model of the antecedents and consequences of satisfaction decisions. Journal of Marketing Research, 17(4), 460-469.
Bhattacherjee, A. (2001). Understanding information systems continuance: An expectation-confirmation model. MIS Quarterly, 25(3), 351-370.
Kano, N., Seraku, N., Takahashi, F., & Tsuji, S. (1984). Attractive quality and must-be quality. Journal of the Japanese Society for Quality Control, 14(2), 39-48.

entries.caveats: What counts as a basic differs by audience and changes over time. The year of the NN/g article is recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Sophisticated products are sparing with charm. One well-placed moment reads as confidence; constant flourish reads as insecurity.

entries.principle: Measure perceived usability and experience with standard questionnaires
entries.claim: The System Usability Scale (SUS; ten items, score 0 to 100) averages about 68 across hundreds of studies, and the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ; 26 items) separates pragmatic scales (perspicuity, efficiency, dependability) from hedonic ones (stimulation, novelty), plus overall attractiveness. Standard instruments are more reliable than home-made ones.
entries.mechanism: A validated questionnaire has known reliability and published benchmarks, so a score can be compared with other products. A home-made question has unknown error and nothing to compare with.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — measurement only
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the instruments measure satisfaction; they do not change it
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — measured, not changed

designMoves: Use SUS for a single number on perceived usability; use the UEQ when look and feel are in question.
Read SUS against its average of 68: a score of 70 is about average, not '70%'.
Collect scores after real tasks and report them beside the task success rate.
Record how experienced each respondent is with the product; experienced users rate higher.
antiPatterns: Reporting SUS as a percentage.
Comparing scores from first-time users with scores from regular users.
A single home-made satisfaction question as the only measure.

howToCheck.human: Administer SUS or the UEQ after a task session. Compare with the published benchmarks.

evidence.strengthNote: Bangor, Kortum and Miller (2008): 2,324 SUS questionnaires from 206 studies, mean about 70. Sauro's benchmark of roughly 500 studies gives an average of 68 (the attribution of that count varies between sources). McLellan, Muddimer and Peres (2012) found that users with more product experience gave higher SUS scores; the size of the difference was not confirmed here. Laugwitz, Held and Schrepp (2008) constructed the UEQ by factor analysis; a benchmark followed in 2017. Hornbæk and Law (2007) found standard questionnaires more reliable than home-made ones. Brooke's original SUS publication (1996) is cited from memory.

sources.citation: Brooke, J. (1996). SUS: A 'quick and dirty' usability scale. In Usability Evaluation in Industry. Taylor & Francis.
Bangor, A., Kortum, P., & Miller, J. (2009). Determining what individual SUS scores mean: Adding an adjective rating scale. Journal of Usability Studies, 4(3), 114-123.
McLellan, S., Muddimer, A., & Peres, S. C. (2012). The effect of experience on System Usability Scale ratings. Journal of Usability Studies, 7(2), 56-67.
Laugwitz, B., Held, T., & Schrepp, M. (2008). Construction and evaluation of a user experience questionnaire. USAB 2008, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 5298, 63-76.

entries.caveats: Questionnaires measure perception, which good looks can inflate (see aesthetic-usability-effect). A personal tool with one user cannot produce a meaningful benchmark comparison; use the items as a structured self-check. Issue and page numbers of the 2009 paper are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: The UEQ's stimulation and novelty scales are the closest standard measure of whether a design feels fresh instead of generic.

entries.principle: Net Promoter Score is a coarse loyalty signal, not a design metric
entries.claim: Net Promoter Score (NPS) is built from one question: how likely are you to recommend this? The claim that it is the single most reliable indicator of company growth did not hold up when independent researchers tested it, and the score does not say what to fix.
entries.mechanism: One question compresses many causes (price, support, brand, product) into one number. The scoring then discards information by sorting answers into three groups.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — measurement only
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the score measures a stated intention
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — NPS does not address ease of use

designMoves: Judge a design change by task success, time, errors and a usability questionnaire, not by NPS.
If NPS is collected, pair it with an open question about the reason, and read the answers.
Compare like with like: the same audience at the same moment in the journey.
antiPatterns: Interrupting a task with a recommend-us survey.
Treating a small movement in NPS as evidence about a redesign.

howToCheck.machine: Flag survey modals that appear before a task is complete.
howToCheck.human: Check that design decisions cite behavioral or usability measures, not NPS alone.

evidence.strengthNote: Keiningham, Cooil, Andreassen and Aksoy (2007), Journal of Marketing: longitudinal data on 21 firms (more than 15,000 interviews according to a secondary source); the authors attempted to replicate the original analyses and found that NPS was not superior to other customer metrics in predicting revenue growth. A practitioner re-analysis (MeasuringU) found that NPS explained some concurrent growth but not future growth. One of the 2007 authors worked for a competing research firm. The original NPS article (Reichheld, 2003) is cited from memory.

sources.citation: Keiningham, T. L., Cooil, B., Andreassen, T. W., & Aksoy, L. (2007). A longitudinal examination of net promoter and firm revenue growth. Journal of Marketing, 71(3), 39-51.
Reichheld, F. F. (2003). The one number you need to grow. Harvard Business Review, 81(12), 46-54.

entries.caveats: NPS can still track broad sentiment over time. It is too blunt for design decisions.

entries.principle: What people prefer and how well they perform are only loosely linked
entries.claim: Preference and measured performance agree on average but diverge often: in one review the correlation was about .44, and across the wider research literature effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction correlate only weakly.
entries.mechanism: Ratings reflect looks, expectations, mood and the memory of peaks and endings. Performance reflects the actual fit between design and task. They are different quantities.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — an insight about measurement
effects.satisfaction: mixed — it can be high where performance is poor, and the reverse
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — perceived ease and actual ease can differ

designMoves: Measure at least one behavioral outcome (success, time, errors) and one subjective outcome in every evaluation.
When they disagree, investigate: a liked but slow design may be polishing over a problem; a fast but disliked one may lack hedonic quality.
Do not choose between Options on stated preference alone when the Options differ in how a task is done.
antiPatterns: Choosing a design by vote.
Declaring success on satisfaction scores without task data.

howToCheck.machine: Scripted task runs give objective completion and step counts to set beside human ratings.
howToCheck.human: Record success and time alongside each rating.

evidence.strengthNote: Nielsen and Levy (1994): 113 comparisons drawn from 57 studies; a correlation of .44 between performance and preference. Hornbæk and Law (2007): 73 studies; correlations of about .25 (effectiveness with efficiency), .20 (efficiency with satisfaction) and .16 (effectiveness with satisfaction). Sauro and Lewis (2009) found stronger correlations (about .44 to .60) in 90 industrial usability tests.

sources.citation: Nielsen, J., & Levy, J. (1994). Measuring usability: Preference vs. performance. Communications of the ACM, 37(4), 66-75.
Hornbæk, K., & Law, E. L.-C. (2007). Meta-analysis of correlations among usability measures. Proceedings of CHI 2007, 617-626.
Sauro, J., & Lewis, J. R. (2009). Correlations among prototypical usability metrics: Evidence for the construct of usability. Proceedings of CHI 2009.

entries.caveats: The correlations are stronger in standard task-based usability tests than across the research literature at large.
entries.sleekRelevance: A design that wins on looks in a side-by-side pick can still lose in use. A picker tool should keep task checks beside taste picks.

entries.principle: Folklore: widely quoted UX statistics that do not survive tracing
entries.claim: '88% of users will not return after a bad experience', 'attention spans are now 8 seconds, shorter than a goldfish's', '53% of mobile visitors leave if a page takes over 3 seconds' and 'every dollar spent on UX returns 100' are each a narrow vendor survey, a misreading or untraceable.
entries.mechanism: A number that sounds precise is easy to quote. As it is copied, the sample, the date and the wording of the original question drop away.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the entry concerns claims, not a design
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the claims do not measure it reliably
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — the claims do not address it

designMoves: State the supported general points in words: bad experiences reduce return visits; slow pages lose visitors; early usability work is cheaper than late fixes.
If a number is needed, measure it on the product in question.
Give the source and its scope with any statistic.
antiPatterns: Any of the four numbers used as a general fact.
A design rationale built on statistics with no primary source.

howToCheck.human: For each statistic in a brief, find who measured it, on whom, when and how.

evidence.strengthNote: 88%: a 2010 white paper by Gomez, a vendor of web-performance services, reporting a commissioned survey of about 1,500 online shoppers; one account gives the wording as referring to shoppers who had abandoned a slow site. 8 seconds: a 2015 Microsoft Canada marketing report cited a statistics website whose sources could not be found; researchers interviewed by the BBC in 2017 called the idea of an average attention span meaningless because attention depends on the task. 53%: Google's 2016 analysis of an opt-in sample of about 3,700 mobile sites; observational, by an advertising company. 1 to 100: usually attributed to Forrester; no primary document was located in this session.

sources.citation: MarketingProfs (2010). Poor web performance hurts brands (report of the Gomez and Equation Research survey).
Maybin, S. (2017). Busting the attention span myth. BBC News, 10 March 2017.
Google / DoubleClick (2016). The need for mobile speed.

entries.caveats: The directions are plausible; the precision is false. The perception-cognition part of this knowledge base holds the better evidence on latency.

entries.principle: Frustration is still common, and most of it repeats
entries.claim: In a 2023 study, people lost 11% to 20% of an hour of computer use to frustrating episodes. They said that 84% of the episodes had happened before and that 87% could happen again, and they could not resolve 26% of them.
entries.mechanism: Frustration arises when a goal is blocked. Recurring causes block goals again and again, and a sense of helplessness grows when the person cannot fix the cause.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — problem solving replaces the task
effects.satisfaction: lowers — and the feeling spreads to the whole product
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — the system stops behaving as predicted

designMoves: List the recurring failure points of each main task and remove them before adding features.
Make every error state say what happened and what to do next.
Provide a way forward from every dead end: retry, back, contact.
Log and review the errors that users hit, not only crashes.
antiPatterns: A generic 'something went wrong' with no action.
Known recurring glitches left in place.
Dead ends without navigation.

howToCheck.machine: Force common failures (offline, timeout, invalid input, empty data) and assert that each renders a specific message and an action.
howToCheck.human: Ask a user to narrate every moment of annoyance during normal use.

evidence.strengthNote: Hertzum and Hornbæk (2023), ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction: 234 crowdsourced participants logged the frustrating episodes they met during one hour of their own computer use. The authors report less time lost than in the central studies from more than 15 years earlier. A self-report diary study of general computer use, not of one product.

sources.citation: Hertzum, M., & Hornbæk, K. (2023). Frustration: Still a common user experience. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 30(3), Article 42.

entries.caveats: Crowd workers may differ from other users. The study does not say which design changes reduce frustration.
entries.sleekRelevance: Composure under failure is part of a premium feel: error, empty and offline states that look and read as designed.

entries.principle: Make actions reversible; forgive mistakes
entries.claim: Interfaces should let people back out of and reverse their actions. Accessibility standards require that legal, financial and data-changing submissions be reversible, checked or confirmed.
entries.mechanism: When mistakes are cheap to reverse, people explore without fear and recover without help. A confirmation dialog interrupts everyone to guard against a rare slip, and people soon click through it by habit; undo protects without interrupting.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no need to double-check every step
effects.satisfaction: raises — a sense of control and safety
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — exploration is safe, so people learn by trying

designMoves: Offer undo for destructive or bulk actions (for example a short undo notice after a delete) in preference to a confirmation dialog.
For legal or financial commitments and for deletion of user data, provide at least one of: reversal, error checking with a chance to correct, or a review step before final submission.
Provide a clearly marked way to leave any state (cancel, close, back) that does not lose work.
Make the browser's back button work at every step.
antiPatterns: Irreversible delete with no confirmation or undo.
Confirmation dialogs on routine, reversible actions.
Flows that break or reset on back.

howToCheck.machine: For each destructive control, assert that an undo control or a confirmation exists. Press back at each step of a flow and assert that state is preserved. Assert that modal dialogs can be closed by keyboard.
howToCheck.human: Try to make and reverse a mistake at each step.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data), Level AA, read from the W3C source. ISO 9241-110:2020 lists controllability and use-error robustness among its interaction principles (principle names recalled; the standard's existence and current status were confirmed by search). Nielsen's heuristic 'user control and freedom' and Shneiderman's rule 'permit easy reversal of actions' are expert guidance. The preference for undo over confirmation is expert opinion, not part of a standard. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility adds supplemental patterns on going back and undoing.

sources.citation: W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data). Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
ISO 9241-110:2020. Ergonomics of human-system interaction - Part 110: Interaction principles.
Nielsen, J. (1994, updated 2020). 10 usability heuristics for user interface design. Nielsen Norman Group.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (patterns: let users go back; make it easy to undo). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: Some actions cannot be undone (sending money, sending a message); those need a review step. WCAG is a legal requirement only where a law adopts it.
entries.sleekRelevance: Calm products rarely ask 'are you sure?'. They let people act and take it back.

entries.principle: Never lose what the user typed or did
entries.claim: Losing entered data through a timeout, a refresh, an error or navigation is among the most damaging interface failures. Accessibility standards require adjustable time limits and forbid asking for the same information twice in one process.
entries.mechanism: Lost work combines wasted effort with a sense of unfairness, and the person must repeat the task with lower motivation. People with cognitive or motor impairments, and anyone who is interrupted, are hit hardest.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — nothing to remember or re-enter
effects.satisfaction: raises — by removing a severe negative peak
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the system behaves the way people assume it does

designMoves: Keep entered data across validation errors, reloads and back navigation.
Save drafts automatically for long input, and show that saving happened.
If a session has a time limit, let the user turn it off, adjust it or extend it, with a warning and at least 20 seconds to respond.
Do not ask again for information already given in the same process; prefill it or offer it for selection.
Warn before navigation that would discard unsaved changes.
antiPatterns: Forms that clear on error.
Silent session expiry.
Asking for an address or email again on a later step.
A long text lost because a submit failed.

howToCheck.machine: Fill a form, trigger a validation error, reload and navigate back; assert that the values persist. Assert a warning on leaving with unsaved changes. Detect session timeouts that give no warning.
howToCheck.human: Start a long form, get interrupted for half an hour, come back.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 success criteria read from the W3C source: 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (Level A), 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A) and 2.2.6 Timeouts (Level AAA: warn users of inactivity limits unless data is kept for more than 20 hours). The W3C note on cognitive accessibility describes data loss and timeouts as barriers in its user stories. Autosave and unsaved-change warnings are expert practice beyond the standard (the Vercel guidelines list the warning). The perception-cognition part covers redundant entry in its entry 'dont-ask-twice'.

sources.citation: W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.3.7 Redundant Entry. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.6 Timeouts. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (pattern: avoid data loss and timeouts). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: Persisting sensitive data (passwords, card numbers) has security limits; the standards make exceptions for security and for essential time limits.
entries.sleekRelevance: Reliability with the user's own input is the quietest and strongest premium signal.

entries.principle: A wait feels shorter when it is explained, bounded and occupied
entries.claim: Unexplained and uncertain waits feel longer than explained, finite ones; feedback extends how long people will wait, and the behavior of a progress indicator changes how long the wait seems. The evidence that skeleton screens shorten perceived waits is mixed.
entries.mechanism: Waiting with no information produces anxiety about whether anything is happening and how long it will last. Information about the cause and the remaining time, and something to look at or do, reduce the attention paid to the passing of time.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no need to wonder whether to retry
effects.satisfaction: raises — perceived duration drops
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the state of the system is clear

designMoves: Show a determinate progress indicator when the duration can be estimated; use an indeterminate one only for short waits.
Say what is happening in plain words.
Design progress so that it does not stall near the end; pacing changes the perceived duration.
Render useful partial content as it arrives.
Use skeleton placeholders to show structure where the layout is known, but do not count on them to make the wait feel shorter.
antiPatterns: A frozen screen with no indicator.
A progress bar that reaches 99% and stops.
A spinner with no text for a long operation.

howToCheck.machine: Throttle the network. Assert that every slow request shows an indicator and that long operations show determinate progress or step text.
howToCheck.human: On a slow connection, note each moment of doubt about whether the system is working.

evidence.strengthNote: Nah (2004): experiment on tolerable waiting time for web information retrieval, about 2 seconds; secondary summaries report that feedback prolonged tolerance. Harrison et al. (2007) showed that the pacing of a progress bar changes perceived duration; Harrison, Yeo and Hudson (2010) found that a bar with backward-moving, decelerating ribbing reduced perceived duration by 11%. Maister (1985) is a set of propositions from service management, not an experiment. Skeleton screens: one small test (Viget, 2017) found them perceived as slower than a spinner; another (Mejtoft et al., 2018) found them perceived as faster; both are small. The perception-cognition part covers progress indicators in its entry 'progress-indicators'.

sources.citation: Nah, F. F.-H. (2004). A study on tolerable waiting time: How long are Web users willing to wait? Behaviour & Information Technology, 23(3), 153-163.
Harrison, C., Yeo, Z., & Hudson, S. E. (2010). Faster progress bars: Manipulating perceived duration with visual augmentations. Proceedings of CHI 2010.
Harrison, C., Amento, B., Kuznetsov, S., & Bell, R. (2007). Rethinking the progress bar. Proceedings of UIST 2007, 115-118.
Maister, D. H. (1985). The psychology of waiting lines.
Viget (2017). A bone to pick with skeleton screens.

entries.caveats: The 2-second figure dates from 2004 and concerns one type of task; expectations have risen since. Tricks that shorten perceived time do not replace real speed.
entries.sleekRelevance: A product that always says what it is doing feels in control. Considered loading states are a hallmark of well-made software.

entries.principle: Interruptions raise stress and frustration even when the work gets done
entries.claim: In a laboratory experiment, people who were interrupted finished tasks faster and about as well, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.
entries.mechanism: After an interruption, people must rebuild their place in the task, and they compensate by working faster. The compensation has an emotional cost. Some people, especially those with attention or memory difficulties, lose their place entirely.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — the context of the task must be rebuilt
effects.satisfaction: lowers — stress and frustration increase
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — unexpected overlays break the predicted flow

designMoves: Do not show modals, sign-up prompts, surveys or chat invitations during a task; wait for a natural break or for the user to ask.
Make notices non-blocking and dismissible; group and delay those that are not urgent.
If an interruption is unavoidable, keep the task state and show where the user was.
Let users turn off non-essential interruptions.
antiPatterns: A newsletter modal on arrival.
Cookie, chat and promotion overlays stacked on each other.
Media that plays by itself.
Tooltips or tours that open unprompted in the middle of a task.

howToCheck.machine: Load each page and wait 30 seconds without input. Flag any overlay, modal or focus change that the user did not initiate. Count simultaneous overlays.
howToCheck.human: Complete the main task and count uninvited interruptions.

evidence.strengthNote: Mark, Gudith and Klocke (2008): laboratory experiment on an email task with interruptions (48 students, according to a secondary source); interrupted work was completed faster with similar quality but with higher stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. A short conference paper, single study. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility recommends limiting interruptions (supplemental guidance).

sources.citation: Mark, G., Gudith, D., & Klocke, U. (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. Proceedings of CHI 2008, 107-110.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (pattern: limit interruptions). Source in the w3c/coga repository.

entries.caveats: The study concerns work tasks and interruptions from other people; marketing overlays are assumed to act in a similar way. Some interruptions are wanted, such as security alerts.
entries.sleekRelevance: Restraint in asking for attention is a signal of class. Premium products wait to be asked.

entries.principle: Deceptive patterns raise short-term conversion and cost trust; many are unlawful
entries.claim: Deceptive patterns (interface designs that steer people into choices they would not otherwise make, also called dark patterns) do increase sign-ups, and they are widespread. Aggressive versions produce strong resentment; mild versions escape notice, which is why regulators target them.
entries.mechanism: The patterns exploit defaults, inattention, obstruction and social pressure. When people notice the manipulation, they infer hostile intent and extend that judgment to the brand.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — users must defend themselves against the interface
effects.satisfaction: lowers — when noticed, with anger at the brand
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — the interface works against the user's goal

designMoves: Make declining as easy and as visible as accepting.
Do not pre-select paid or data-sharing options.
Make canceling as easy as subscribing, in the same channel.
Show only truthful scarcity and urgency; no fake timers or stock counts.
Word choices neutrally; no guilt-inducing text on the decline option.
State renewal terms before commitment.
antiPatterns: Confirmshaming ('No thanks, I like paying more').
Hidden or grayed-out decline buttons.
Pre-ticked add-ons.
Countdown timers that reset.
Cancellation that requires a phone call.

howToCheck.machine: Compare the visual weight (size, contrast) of accept and decline controls. Flag pre-checked optional checkboxes. Detect countdown timers that restart on reload. Count the steps to subscribe and the steps to cancel.
howToCheck.human: Try to decline every offer and to cancel. Note anything that felt like a trick.

evidence.strengthNote: Luguri and Strahilevitz (2021): two large experiments with samples representative of US consumers; mild dark patterns more than doubled acceptance of a dubious service and aggressive ones nearly quadrupled it; aggressive patterns caused a strong backlash and mild ones did not; less educated participants were more susceptible to mild patterns. Mathur et al. (2019): a crawl of about 11,000 shopping sites found 1,818 instances on 1,254 sites (about 11.1%). A 2024 sweep by consumer-protection agencies from 26 countries found that about 76% of 642 subscription sites and apps used at least one dark pattern. Law: Article 25 of the EU Digital Services Act prohibits online platforms from designing interfaces that deceive or manipulate users, and US regulators pursue such designs as unfair or deceptive practices; these legal points are stated from memory and were not re-checked, and US rules on subscription cancellation were unsettled in 2025 and 2026.

sources.citation: Luguri, J., & Strahilevitz, L. J. (2021). Shining a light on dark patterns. Journal of Legal Analysis, 13(1), 43-109.

Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark patterns at scale: Findings from a crawl of 11K shopping websites. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81.
ICPEN (2024). Sweep finds majority of websites and mobile apps use dark patterns in the marketing of subscription services.
Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act), Article 25: Online interface design and organisation.

entries.caveats: Because mild patterns provoke no backlash, the business incentive to use them is real; the reasons not to use them are ethical and legal. Legal exposure varies by jurisdiction. This entry is not legal advice.
entries.sleekRelevance: Trustworthy products look and behave straightforwardly. Manufactured urgency and guilt copy are strong markers of low-quality commerce.

entries.principle: More options hurt only under specific conditions
entries.claim: Across experiments, the average effect of offering more options on satisfaction or on choosing is close to zero. Large sets do harm when the options are complex or hard to compare, the task is difficult, people do not know what they want, and they aim to decide quickly.
entries.mechanism: Comparing options costs effort and raises the fear of choosing wrongly. When people have clear preferences or the options are easy to compare, a large set simply improves the odds of a good match.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — raises with unstructured, hard-to-compare sets; changes little with organized ones
effects.satisfaction: mixed — depends on the four moderating conditions
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — when options lack an obvious order or a recommended choice

designMoves: Reduce the difficulty of choosing before reducing the number of options: put options into categories, make them comparable on the same attributes, and order them meaningfully.
Mark a recommended or default option when users are unlikely to have a preference.
For newcomers and one-off decisions, show a short curated set with access to the rest.
For experts with known needs, give the full set with filtering and search.
antiPatterns: Long unsorted lists of similar items.
Plans or products that differ on attributes that cannot be compared.
Options that experienced users need, removed in the name of simplicity.

howToCheck.machine: Count options per decision point. Flag sets above a threshold the Catalog sets that lack grouping, sorting, filtering or a marked default.
howToCheck.human: Ask a newcomer to pick. Note hesitation, and whether they can explain the differences between the options.

evidence.strengthNote: Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd (2010): 63 conditions from 50 experiments, N = 5,036; mean effect virtually zero, with large variance between studies. Chernev, Böckenholt and Goodman (2015): 99 observations, N = 7,202; four moderators (choice set complexity, decision task difficulty, preference uncertainty, decision goal) reliably predict when overload occurs. The famous jam study (Iyengar and Lepper, 2000) is cited from memory. The perception-cognition part of this knowledge base has a parallel entry, 'choice-overload'.

sources.citation: Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R., & Todd, P. M. (2010). Can there ever be too many options? A meta-analytic review of choice overload. Journal of Consumer Research, 37(3), 409-425.
Chernev, A., Böckenholt, U., & Goodman, J. (2015). Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 25(2), 333-358.
Iyengar, S. S., & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995-1006.

entries.caveats: 'Fewer options is always better' is folklore. So is 'choice overload is a myth': under the four conditions it is reliable.
entries.sleekRelevance: Curation signals confidence, but the evidence favors making choice easy over making it small. A picker with three or four clearly different Options per Step fits the conditions under which choice works.

entries.principle: Most people keep the default
entries.claim: A pre-selected option is chosen far more often than the same option presented without pre-selection. The effect is large on average and varies widely by context.
entries.mechanism: Three routes: effort (keeping the default is easier), endorsement (people read the default as the designer's recommendation) and endowment (the default feels like the status quo, and giving it up feels like a loss).

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — one decision fewer
effects.satisfaction: raises — when the default suits the person; lowers when a self-serving default is discovered
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — things work without configuration

designMoves: Set each default to what suits most of the audience, and say that it is recommended when it is.
Never use defaults for choices that benefit the provider at the user's cost (paid add-ons, marketing consent).
Make every default easy to see and change.
Record whether a value was chosen or defaulted, so that later decisions can tell the difference.
antiPatterns: Pre-checked consent or upsell boxes.
Defaults that favor the vendor.
No default where one option is clearly right for most people.

howToCheck.machine: List every pre-selected input. Flag pre-selected inputs tied to payment, consent or data sharing.
howToCheck.human: Review each default: would the typical user thank you for it?

evidence.strengthNote: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber and Johnson (2019): 58 studies, pooled N = 73,675; d = 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.53 to 0.83), with substantial variation; some studies showed no effect and two showed a negative one. Defaults were stronger in consumer domains and when they worked through endorsement or endowment. Johnson and Goldstein (2003) on organ-donation defaults is the classic demonstration, cited from memory.

sources.citation: Jachimowicz, J. M., Duncan, S., Weber, E. U., & Johnson, E. J. (2019). When and why defaults influence decisions: A meta-analysis of default effects. Behavioural Public Policy, 3(2), 159-186.
Johnson, E. J., & Goldstein, D. (2003). Do defaults save lives? Science, 302(5649), 1338-1339.

entries.caveats: Power brings responsibility: pre-selected consent is unlawful in some jurisdictions, and a self-serving default is a deceptive pattern.
entries.sleekRelevance: Well-made products feel right out of the box. Good defaults are how a tool feels considered before the user has done anything.

entries.principle: People want to feel in control, yet few customize
entries.claim: Feeling that one acts by one's own choice (autonomy) supports motivation and wellbeing, and control is a formal usability principle. Most people nevertheless leave settings as they are, and making or configuring something raises attachment only when the effort succeeds.
entries.mechanism: Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence and relatedness as basic psychological needs. Control over pace and outcome satisfies autonomy; being forced, rushed or surprised frustrates it. Customizing costs effort now for an uncertain later benefit, so people postpone it. When they do build something successfully, they value it more (the IKEA effect).

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — control lowers anxiety; many settings raise load
effects.satisfaction: raises — with a sense of control; unused options add nothing
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when the user sets the pace and can go back

designMoves: Let the user start, pause, skip and go back at their own pace; avoid forced sequences and content that advances by itself.
Offer a few meaningful settings (theme, density, notification level) instead of many trivial ones.
Make the defaults good enough that no one needs the settings.
Where the user makes or configures something, make early success easy; a failed setup removes the benefit.
antiPatterns: Forced tours.
Carousels that advance by themselves.
A settings page standing in for design decisions.
Customization that can leave the product broken.

howToCheck.machine: Flag auto-advancing carousels and timed transitions. Verify that skip and back controls exist in multi-step flows. Verify that user preferences persist.
howToCheck.human: Ask after onboarding: did you ever feel pushed?

evidence.strengthNote: Norton, Mochon and Ariely (2012): four studies (IKEA boxes, origami, Lego sets); labor raised valuation only when the build was completed successfully. Self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000), its application to digital experience (Peters, Calvo and Ryan, 2018) and Mackay's (1991) study of why people do not customize software are cited from memory and were not re-checked. ISO 9241-110:2020 lists controllability as an interaction principle (name recalled). Direct experiments on autonomy in everyday interfaces are fewer than the general support for the theory.

sources.citation: Norton, M. I., Mochon, D., & Ariely, D. (2012). The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 22(3), 453-460.
Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68-78.
Peters, D., Calvo, R. A., & Ryan, R. M. (2018). Designing for motivation, engagement and wellbeing in digital experience. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 797.
Mackay, W. E. (1991). Triggers and barriers to customizing software. Proceedings of CHI '91, 153-160.

entries.caveats: More control is not always better: many choices and settings shift work to the user.
entries.sleekRelevance: A premium product feels deferential: it follows the user's pace and system preferences and offers a few well-chosen controls.

entries.principle: Same thing, same look, same place, same name
entries.claim: Components with the same function should be identified the same way, and repeated navigation and help should appear in the same relative order across pages; this is a formal accessibility requirement and a long-standing usability heuristic. Consistency is a means to serve users' tasks, not a goal in itself.
entries.mechanism: Consistency lets people reuse what they learned on the first screen. Each inconsistency forces a check: is this the same thing or a different one? Internal consistency is agreement within a product; external consistency is agreement with platform and web conventions.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — learning transfers between screens
effects.satisfaction: raises — predictability, which also reads as care
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the second screen feels known

designMoves: Define each component once (tokens for color, type, spacing, radius, shadow) and reuse it; allow no page-level overrides.
Keep navigation, search and help in the same order and place on every page.
Use the same label and icon for the same function everywhere.
Follow platform conventions for standard controls.
Allow a deliberate inconsistency only where the user's task differs.
antiPatterns: Two styles of primary button.
The same action named differently on different pages.
Navigation order that changes between sections.
Icons that mean different things in different places.

howToCheck.machine: Across pages, compare the order of navigation links and the computed styles of components with the same role. Flag differing labels for links with the same destination. Count distinct values per token category.
howToCheck.human: Open three pages side by side. List anything that changed without a reason.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 success criteria, read from the W3C source: 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation (Level AA), 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (Level AA) and 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A). Nielsen's heuristic 'consistency and standards' (1994) is expert guidance. Grudin (1989) argued in a peer-reviewed essay that consistency is an unreliable primary goal and that fitting the user's work matters more; violations of consistency can improve performance.

sources.citation: W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.4 Consistent Identification. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.6 Consistent Help. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
Grudin, J. (1989). The case against user interface consistency. Communications of the ACM, 32(10), 1164-1173.
Nielsen, J. (1994, updated 2020). 10 usability heuristics for user interface design. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: The same control may rightly differ in two contexts if the tasks differ. Consistency with a poor convention preserves the poor convention. The WCAG criteria cover navigation, identification and help; consistency of visual styling is good practice beyond the standard.
entries.sleekRelevance: Visual consistency is the most checkable component of a refined look. A small token set applied without exception is what makes a product look designed by one mind.

entries.principle: Always show what the system is doing and what just happened
entries.claim: Interfaces should keep people informed through timely feedback: every action gets a visible response, and every state (loading, empty, error, success, disabled) is shown.
entries.mechanism: People act, then check the result to decide the next step. Without feedback they cannot tell success from failure, so they repeat the action or give up. Feedback closes the loop between intention and outcome.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no guessing about state
effects.satisfaction: raises — confidence that actions worked
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — cause and effect are visible

designMoves: Give every control hover, focus, pressed, loading and disabled states.
Confirm completed actions where the user is looking (inline, or next to the control).
Design empty, loading, error and success states for every view that fetches data.
Keep a button's label while it loads, and add an indicator.
Announce status changes to assistive technology (polite live regions).
antiPatterns: Clicks with no visible response.
Silent failures.
Blank screens for empty or loading data.
Success shown only by the absence of an error.

howToCheck.machine: For each interactive element, assert distinct computed styles for hover, focus and active. Trigger each asynchronous action and assert that a loading state and then a success or error state appears. Assert aria-live regions for status messages.
howToCheck.human: After each action ask: did it work? How do you know?

evidence.strengthNote: The first of Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, refined in 1994 from a factor analysis of 249 usability problems and unchanged since. ISO 9241-110:2020 includes self-descriptiveness as an interaction principle (name recalled). The W3C note on cognitive accessibility asks for rapid feedback as supplemental guidance. The specific state lists and timings in practice guides are vendor conventions (the Vercel guidelines were read in this session).

sources.citation: Nielsen, J. (1994, updated 2020). 10 usability heuristics for user interface design. Nielsen Norman Group.

W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force (2021). Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities (pattern: provide feedback). Source in the w3c/coga repository.
Vercel. Web Interface Guidelines. vercel-labs/web-interface-guidelines repository.

entries.caveats: Too much feedback becomes noise: confirm what matters and keep routine acknowledgments subtle.
entries.sleekRelevance: Complete, quiet state design, including the unglamorous empty and error states, is what makes an interface feel finished.

entries.principle: Nothing should move or change context unless the user asked
entries.claim: Receiving focus or changing a setting must not trigger an unexpected change of context, and content should not shift position unexpectedly. The first two are Level A accessibility requirements; the third is a measured web quality metric.
entries.mechanism: People aim at where things are and plan from what they see. If the page moves or navigates unprompted, the action lands on the wrong target and the plan is void. Predictability is what makes an interface trustworthy at the level of the hand.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — no re-orientation
effects.satisfaction: raises — fewer wrong taps and surprises
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the interface does what was expected and nothing else

designMoves: Do not navigate, submit or open windows on focus or on selection; use an explicit button.
Reserve space for images, embeds, fonts and late content so that layout does not shift (Cumulative Layout Shift at or under 0.1).
Keep controls in place while content updates; do not insert content above what the user is reading.
Do not move focus without a user action.
antiPatterns: Select menus that navigate on change.
Banners that push content down after load.
Buttons that move as the user reaches for them.
Forms that submit by themselves.

howToCheck.machine: Measure Cumulative Layout Shift. Tab through the page and assert that focus triggers no navigation or new window. Change each select, radio and checkbox and assert no change of context. Compare element positions before and after late loads.
howToCheck.human: Try to tap a control while the page is loading.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 success criteria 3.2.1 On Focus and 3.2.2 On Input (both Level A), read from the W3C source. The Cumulative Layout Shift threshold of 0.1 for 'good' is Google's Core Web Vitals convention, read from the web-vitals library documentation; it is a vendor metric, not a standard. The W3C note on cognitive accessibility includes a pattern that controls and content do not move unexpectedly.

sources.citation: W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.1 On Focus. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 3.2.2 On Input. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
Google Chrome team. web-vitals library, README (rating thresholds for CLS, INP and LCP).

entries.caveats: A change of context on input is allowed when the user has been told beforehand. Cumulative Layout Shift measures only unexpected shifts.
entries.sleekRelevance: Stillness is a luxury signal. Pages that load into place without jumping feel engineered.

entries.principle: People react badly to sudden change in products they know
entries.claim: Redesigns of familiar products produce a short-term negative reaction (change aversion), which preparation, explanation, a way to switch back and follow-through reduce. A reaction that persists signals a real loss of capability or efficiency.
entries.mechanism: Regular users have invested in learning where things are. A redesign destroys that investment at once and hands them a relearning task they did not choose. The loss is felt immediately, and the benefits are not yet visible.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — existing users must relearn
effects.satisfaction: lowers — at first; it recovers if the new design serves their tasks better
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: lowers — the familiar has been removed

designMoves: Change in steps where possible; keep the locations and names of frequent functions.
Tell users what will change and why, before and after the change.
Offer a period in which users can switch between old and new.
Ask for feedback and act on it visibly.
Measure task performance after the change settles, not only sentiment in the first week.
antiPatterns: A full visual and structural overhaul released at once without notice.
Removing a workflow that users rely on.
Dismissing every complaint as change aversion.

howToCheck.machine: Compare the labels and positions of the most used functions between versions. Flag renamed or moved frequent functions.
howToCheck.human: Ask experienced users to do their three most frequent tasks on the new version.

evidence.strengthNote: Sedley and Müller (2013) is a Google case study in a conference's extended abstracts: applying a change-management approach to the Google Drive launch produced more positive user perceptions than earlier redesign launches; the authors call for controlled experiments. Public cases fit the pattern: Snap reported a fall in daily users from 191 to 188 million after its 2018 redesign, which drew a petition of about 1.2 million signatures, and its chief executive attributed lower usage partly to disruption from the redesign (news reports). Case evidence, not experiments.

sources.citation: Sedley, A., & Müller, H. (2013). Minimizing change aversion for the Google Drive launch. CHI '13 Extended Abstracts, 2351-2354.
MacRumors (2018). Snapchat's recent redesign resulted in millions of lost users (news report, 7 August 2018).

entries.caveats: Applies to existing users of an existing product; a new product has no change aversion to manage. A short-term outcry does not show that a change was wrong.
entries.sleekRelevance: Sophisticated products evolve their look gradually. Abrupt restyling is costly even when the new style is better.

entries.principle: The appeal of novelty is temporary; usefulness and meaning last
entries.claim: Early in ownership, people's good experiences relate mostly to stimulation and to learning the product; over weeks they relate to usefulness and to how the product fits their life. Reactions to new features in live tests are also inflated at first by a novelty effect.
entries.mechanism: Hedonic adaptation: people get used to pleasant new stimuli, and the response fades. What remains is what the product does for them every day.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the finding concerns the course of time
effects.satisfaction: mixed — novelty lifts early ratings; lasting satisfaction needs usefulness
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — over time, as familiarity grows

designMoves: Judge expressive choices by how they will feel on the hundredth use: favor qualities that last (clarity, speed, good typography) over effects that surprise.
Keep striking effects off high-frequency paths.
Evaluate a redesign after the novelty period; numbers from the first week mislead in both directions.
Invest in the parts people use daily.
antiPatterns: Launch-day effects that slow routine use.
Deciding on a change from the first days of data.

howToCheck.machine: Flag long or decorative animations on actions marked as frequent.
howToCheck.human: Revisit a design after two weeks of daily use. List what has become annoying and what still pleases.

evidence.strengthNote: Karapanos, Zimmerman, Forlizzi and Martens (2009): a five-week study of six people who bought an iPhone; early experiences related mostly to hedonic aspects, and prolonged experiences to how the product became meaningful in the person's life. A very small qualitative sample and one product. The novelty effect in online experiments is described by Kohavi and colleagues (2012), cited from memory. Sauer and Sonderegger report that the influence of aesthetics in one-off tests wanes over time.

sources.citation: Karapanos, E., Zimmerman, J., Forlizzi, J., & Martens, J.-B. (2009). User experience over time: An initial framework. Proceedings of CHI 2009, 729-738.
Kohavi, R., Deng, A., Frasca, B., Longbotham, R., Walker, T., & Xu, Y. (2012). Trustworthy online controlled experiments: Five puzzling outcomes explained. Proceedings of KDD 2012.

entries.caveats: Some aesthetic qualities keep giving pleasure: beauty ratings were stable in Hassenzahl's study. The claim concerns novelty specifically.
entries.sleekRelevance: Timeless-feeling products choose restraint because it survives repetition. The test of a signature element is whether it is still welcome after a month.

entries.principle: Two kinds of visual appeal: classical order and expressive originality
entries.claim: People perceive website aesthetics along two dimensions: classical (orderly, clear design) and expressive (creativity, originality and the breaking of design conventions). The classical dimension is close to what usability experts recommend.
entries.mechanism: Classical qualities make a page easy to process. Expressive qualities show the designer's originality and supply interest. People judge the two separately.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — on the classical dimension; expressive elements can raise it
effects.satisfaction: raises — both dimensions contribute to appeal
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — with classical quality

designMoves: Secure classical quality first: alignment, clear grouping, consistent spacing, restrained color.
Add expressive quality in a controlled amount and place (see maya-typicality-novelty).
Rate a design on both dimensions separately. A high classical score with a low expressive score is the 'clean but generic' profile.
antiPatterns: Expressive effects on a disorderly base.
Classical order with no expressive element where distinctiveness is the goal.

howToCheck.machine: Classical proxies: regularity of alignment, consistency of spacing, number of colors. Expressive quality has no reliable automatic measure.
howToCheck.human: Rate the page with the classical and expressive scales (five items each) of Lavie and Tractinsky.

evidence.strengthNote: Lavie and Tractinsky (2004): four studies with exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses produced the two dimensions, each measured by a five-item scale with adequate reliability and validity. A measurement paper: it shows how people perceive, not which mix is best. The relation of each dimension to perceived usability was not confirmed in this session.

sources.citation: Lavie, T., & Tractinsky, N. (2004). Assessing dimensions of perceived visual aesthetics of web sites. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 60(3), 269-298.

entries.caveats: Later instruments divide aesthetics differently (four facets in the VisAWI; see craftsmanship-facet). The right mix depends on genre and audience.
entries.sleekRelevance: Names the gap precisely: generated interfaces usually score acceptably on classical order and low on expressive quality.

entries.principle: Treat platform vendors' claims for expressive styles as claims
entries.claim: Google reported that its Material 3 Expressive designs let people spot key interface elements up to four times faster (46 internal studies, more than 18,000 participants), while Apple's Liquid Glass (2025) drew criticism for reduced legibility and Apple added controls to tone it down. Expressive styling has real benefits and real costs, and both depend on execution.
entries.mechanism: Bolder contrast of size, color and shape makes key elements stand out (salience). Translucency and layered effects lower the contrast between text and what lies behind it, which makes reading harder.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — stronger emphasis lowers search effort; translucent layers raise reading effort
effects.satisfaction: mixed — some users find expressive styles fresh; others find them tiring or hard to read
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: mixed — clearer emphasis helps; see-through or unstable surfaces hurt

designMoves: Borrow the supported part of expressive styling: make the single most important action clearly larger and more contrasting.
Keep text on opaque or nearly opaque surfaces; test translucent surfaces over the busiest content they will sit on.
Respect the reduce-transparency and contrast preferences of the system.
Do not adopt a platform's newest style on the strength of its launch claims; wait for independent evaluation.
antiPatterns: Text over blurred or moving backgrounds without a contrast check.
A platform restyle adopted wholesale in a cross-platform web product.
Citing '4x faster' as a general property of expressive design.

howToCheck.machine: Compute worst-case text contrast over translucent surfaces by sampling the composited pixels behind the text. Verify handling of prefers-reduced-transparency and prefers-contrast.
howToCheck.human: Read interface text over varied content. Check that the primary action is found at a glance.

evidence.strengthNote: Google's figures come from its own announcement and from press coverage; a first version of the blog post was published early and withdrawn, the methods are not public, and 'up to 4x' describes the best case (the example given is an email send button). The critique of Liquid Glass by NN/g (Budiu, October 2025) is expert review, known here through secondary coverage. Apple added a 'Tinted' option in iOS 26.1 and, according to reviews, a transparency slider with a more tinted default in iOS 27 (2026); these product changes are reported by news and review sites and were not checked against Apple's documentation.

sources.citation: Google Design (2025). Better, easier, emotional UX (article on the research behind Material 3 Expressive).
Dezeen (2025). Google ushers in age of expressive interfaces with Material Design update (28 May 2025).
Budiu, R. (2025). Liquid Glass is cracked, and usability suffers in iOS 26. Nielsen Norman Group (as reported by OSnews).
MacStories (2026). iOS and iPadOS 27: The MacStories review.

entries.caveats: Vendor research may be sound; it is unpublished and self-interested. The reception of a style in its first year also includes change aversion.
entries.sleekRelevance: Glass effects and expressive shapes can read as modern, but their premium effect depends on flawless legibility. The Liquid Glass episode shows the cost of getting that wrong at the highest level of craft.

entries.principle: Color-emotion associations are broadly shared across cultures, with local differences
entries.claim: People in 30 nations associated color words with emotions in highly similar ways (average similarity r = .88), with systematic differences by nation, language and geography. A shared association is not a fixed meaning or an effect on behavior, so the popular rule that each color has one universal meaning goes beyond the evidence.
entries.mechanism: Associations come from shared human experience (blood, sky, night, sun) and from language and culture. A color therefore evokes a family of emotions, some of them opposite in tone (red: love and anger), and context selects among them.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — associations do not change effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the study measured associations, not satisfaction
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when color roles follow widely learned interface conventions, such as red for errors

designMoves: Use color meaning as a tendency, and check it for the specific audience.
Rely on conventions learned from interfaces themselves (red for destructive actions or errors, green for success) more than on claimed emotional effects.
Never use color as the only carrier of meaning.
Test the palette with members of the audience when the audience belongs to another culture.
antiPatterns: Choosing a brand color from a chart of color meanings.
Assuming that white, red or green mean the same everywhere.
Claims that a hue causes trust or purchases.

howToCheck.machine: Verify that status colors are accompanied by icons or text. Verify that semantic color tokens map consistently to roles.
howToCheck.human: Ask audience members which three words the palette suggests.

evidence.strengthNote: Jonauskaite et al. (2020), Psychological Science: 4,598 participants from 30 nations, tested in 22 languages; participants linked 12 color terms to 20 emotions. Similarity was higher for nations close in language or geography, and a machine-learning analysis could predict nation from the pattern of associations. The study measured associations to color words, not to colors on a screen, and not behavior. The review by Elliot and Maier (2014) covers effects of color on psychological functioning; only its citation was confirmed here.

sources.citation: Jonauskaite, D., et al. (2020). Universal patterns in color-emotion associations are further shaped by linguistic and geographic proximity. Psychological Science, 31(10), 1245-1260.
Elliot, A. J., & Maier, M. A. (2014). Color psychology: Effects of perceiving color on psychological functioning in humans. Annual Review of Psychology, 65, 95-120.

entries.caveats: The folklore version (blue means trust, red creates urgency, green means go, everywhere and reliably) is not what this evidence shows. A similarity of r = .88 still leaves room for important local exceptions, such as the colors of mourning.
entries.sleekRelevance: Refined palettes are chosen for fit and execution, not for symbolism. The research gives no hue a claim to sophistication.

entries.principle: Lightness and saturation shape feeling more than hue does
entries.claim: In a classic study, brighter colors were rated more pleasant and more saturated colors more arousing. These two properties had stronger and more consistent effects on emotion ratings than hue.
entries.mechanism: Brightness and saturation are dimensions of intensity that the visual system registers directly. Hue associations are more learned and depend more on context.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — highly saturated areas compete for attention
effects.satisfaction: mixed — pleasantness rises with brightness; high saturation excites more than it pleases
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; no direct effect is expected

designMoves: Decide the lightness and saturation range of the palette before the hue: a calm interface comes from moderate saturation and controlled lightness steps, whatever the hue.
Use high saturation in small areas for emphasis, not for large surfaces.
Derive neutrals and tints in a perceptually uniform color space so that lightness steps are even.
When two palettes feel different, compare their saturation and lightness before blaming the hue.
antiPatterns: Large, fully saturated backgrounds.
Many accents at equal saturation.
Swapping the hue to fix a palette that is too loud.

howToCheck.machine: Convert the palette and samples of rendered pixels to a perceptual color space (for example OKLCH). Report the share of the viewport above a chroma threshold and the evenness of the lightness steps.
howToCheck.human: Does the page feel calm or loud at arm's length?

evidence.strengthNote: Valdez and Mehrabian (1994), Journal of Experimental Psychology: General: ratings of Munsell color chips; the standardized regression weights were .69 (brightness) and .22 (saturation) for pleasure, and -.31 (brightness) and .60 (saturation) for arousal. Blue, blue-green, green, red-purple, purple and purple-blue were rated most pleasant, and yellow and green-yellow least. Isolated chips rated three decades ago. On websites, colorfulness mattered less than visual complexity for first impressions (Reinecke et al., 2013).

sources.citation: Valdez, P., & Mehrabian, A. (1994). Effects of color on emotions. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 123(4), 394-409.
