Reinecke, K., Yeh, T., Miratrix, L., Mardiko, R., Zhao, Y., Liu, J., & Gajos, K. Z. (2013). Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics with a quantification of perceived visual complexity and colorfulness. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 2049-2058.

entries.caveats: The ratings concern single color chips, not interfaces. The preferred level of colorfulness differs by audience (see preferences-vary-by-audience).
entries.sleekRelevance: The restrained look associated with premium interfaces is largely a decision about saturation and lightness: quiet neutrals and one controlled accent.

entries.principle: A color works when it fits the product and the audience
entries.claim: Color changes how a brand's personality is perceived, and the appeal of a website's colors affects trust and satisfaction differently across cultures.
entries.mechanism: People judge whether a color is appropriate for what is being offered. A fitting color is processed easily and supports the intended personality; an unfitting one creates doubt.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — not about effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — when the colors appeal to that audience
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; no direct effect is expected

designMoves: State the intended personality in two or three words, then test candidate palettes against those words with the audience.
Check the genre: which colors do the audience's trusted examples use, and is the departure deliberate?
Vary lightness and saturation as well as hue when exploring options.
Re-test color choices for each cultural audience.
antiPatterns: A brand color picked by personal taste alone.
The sector's dominant color copied without a decision.
A tool's default accent.

howToCheck.machine: Detect whether the accent equals a known framework default (for example a default indigo or blue).
howToCheck.human: Ask audience members to choose words for the palette from a list that includes the intended ones.

evidence.strengthNote: Labrecque and Milne (2012): four studies on how color relates to brand personality, purchase intent and likability; secondary summaries report that red read as exciting and blue as competent and that saturation and lightness also shifted perceptions. Cyr, Head and Larios (2010): three color treatments of a website (blue, yellow, gray) tested with three culturally distinct groups using a survey, eyetracking and interviews; color appeal significantly predicted trust and satisfaction, with differences across cultures (the specific countries were not confirmed in this session). The effects concern perceptions and intentions, not purchases.

sources.citation: Labrecque, L. I., & Milne, G. R. (2012). Exciting red and competent blue: The importance of color in marketing. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, 40(5), 711-727.
Cyr, D., Head, M., & Larios, H. (2010). Colour appeal in website design within and across cultures: A multi-method evaluation. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 68(1-2), 1-21.

entries.caveats: Associations such as 'blue is competent' come from specific samples and logos; they are tendencies. Fit can be learned: a brand can own an unusual color through consistent use.
entries.sleekRelevance: An accent that is clearly chosen, and is not the framework default, is one of the cheapest bespoke signals.

entries.principle: Folklore: 'color increases brand recognition by 80%' and '62-90% of product judgments are based on color'
entries.claim: Neither statistic has a traceable primary study. The 80% figure is attributed to a university study that nobody produces; the 62-90% figure appears in a 2006 review article that reports no data of its own.
entries.mechanism: A number that sounds precise travels from article to article with a citation that leads only to another article.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the entry concerns claims, not a design
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the claims measure nothing reliably
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — the claims do not address it

designMoves: Do not cite these numbers.

Use the supported statements: color shifts perceived brand personality and fit; lightness and saturation affect emotional tone; color appeal relates to trust and satisfaction in a way that depends on culture.
Decide color by fit and by testing with the audience.
antiPatterns: A palette justified with either statistic.
The inference that color outweighs content, price or usability.

howToCheck.human: Ask for the primary source of any color statistic.

evidence.strengthNote: The 80% claim is usually credited to a 'University of Loyola, Maryland' study; the sites that repeat it give no publication, and one trace suggests the original wording compared color with black-and-white material. The 62-90% claim (with 'within 90 seconds') appears in the abstract of Singh (2006), Management Decision, a narrative review; the origin of the range was not found in this session.

sources.citation: Color Matters / Colorcom. Why color matters (web page that repeats the 80% claim without a publication).
Singh, S. (2006). Impact of color on marketing. Management Decision, 44(6), 783-789.

entries.caveats: Color does matter; the three supported entries in this topic say how.

entries.principle: People tend to prefer curved contours, moderately and not universally
entries.claim: Across studies, people prefer curved over angular shapes with a medium-sized effect. The preference depends on how long people look, what is shown, the task and the viewer's expertise.
entries.mechanism: Two accounts exist: sharp angles may signal threat and be disliked, or curves may be liked in their own right. The evidence favors liking for curves. Familiarity and context can outweigh either.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — not about effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — slightly, on average, for curved forms
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — no evidence that roundness aids use

designMoves: Treat corner radius as a choice of personality (softer or sharper), make it deliberately and apply it consistently.
Keep radii proportionate: nested shapes should look parallel, which means the inner radius equals the outer radius minus the gap between them.
Do not expect rounding to improve usability or trust.
Avoid one uniform large radius on everything; it is a common default look.
antiPatterns: Mixed radii with no system.
The claim that rounded buttons convert better, stated as a general fact.
Rounding as the only expression of the brand.

howToCheck.machine: Collect all computed border-radius values. Flag more than a set number of distinct values. Flag nested elements whose radii are not concentric.
howToCheck.human: Does the shape language match the intended personality?

evidence.strengthNote: Chuquichambi et al. (2022): 61 studies, 106 independent samples, 309 effect sizes; Hedges' g = 0.39, moderated by presentation time, stimulus type, expertise and task; the authors conclude that the preference is reliable but not universal. Bar and Neta (2006) is the well-known early demonstration with everyday objects. Bertamini et al. (2016) concluded that the effect reflects liking for curvature, not dislike of angles. The stimuli are objects, abstract shapes and interiors, not interfaces. The concentric-radius rule is a craft convention, not a research finding.

sources.citation: Chuquichambi, E. G., Vartanian, O., Skov, M., Corradi, G. B., Nadal, M., Silvia, P. J., & Munar, E. (2022). How universal is preference for visual curvature? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1518(1), 151-165.
Bar, M., & Neta, M. (2006). Humans prefer curved visual objects. Psychological Science, 17(8), 645-648.
Bertamini, M., Palumbo, L., Gheorghes, T. N., & Galatsidas, M. (2016). Do observers like curvature or do they dislike angularity? British Journal of Psychology, 107(1), 154-178.

entries.caveats: Design-trained viewers and longer viewing change the pattern. Sharp geometry can signal precision or seriousness in the right genre. The step from shape preference to interface corner radius is an extrapolation. Volume and pages of the Bar and Neta paper are recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: Radius is a quick way to set tone, and uniform heavy rounding is now a marker of default styling. Precision in how radii relate reads as craft more than the amount of rounding does.

entries.principle: Folklore: 'the golden ratio makes layouts beautiful'
entries.claim: Controlled studies do not find a reliable preference for the golden ratio (about 1.618 to 1) over nearby proportions. Preferences for proportions vary between people.
entries.mechanism: The idea persists because the ratio is mathematically elegant and because it can be found, after the fact, in almost any admired object if one chooses where to measure.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — a proportion within a normal range does not change effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — no reliable effect has been shown
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — no evidence of any effect

designMoves: Choose proportions and type scales for fit with the content and for consistency; any consistent ratio gives order.
Use a modular scale if it helps keep sizes consistent, without attributing special power to 1.618.
Do not adjust a layout to hit the ratio at the cost of content.
antiPatterns: Layout decisions justified by the golden ratio.
Spirals overlaid on finished designs as proof of quality.

howToCheck.machine: Check that type sizes and spacing follow one consistent scale, whatever its ratio.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether the proportions suit the content.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the popular claim. Stieger and Swami (2015) found no explicit or implicit preference for the golden ratio in art pictures and suggested that any preference depends on art expertise. Earlier reviews of research on rectangle preference reached similar conclusions (recalled, not re-checked).

sources.citation: Stieger, S., & Swami, V. (2015). Time to let go? No automatic aesthetic preference for the golden ratio in art pictures. Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 9(1), 91-100.

entries.caveats: A consistent system of proportions does help. The specific number does not matter.
entries.sleekRelevance: Order comes from consistency of scale, not from a magic number.

entries.principle: Generative AI raises individual output quality and lowers variety across outputs
entries.claim: In experiments, people who used generative AI for ideas produced work that was rated better individually, but their outputs resembled each other more. Different large language models (LLMs) also give responses that are more alike than the responses of different people.
entries.mechanism: A model generates what is most probable given its training data, so it favors the center of the distribution. Many users who draw on the same few models start from similar suggestions, and people tend to anchor on the first suggestion they see.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — the model supplies a ready starting point
effects.satisfaction: mixed — each result looks competent; the set looks alike
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — central, familiar patterns are easy to use

designMoves: Do not ask a model for an open-ended design; give it decisions (specific type, color, layout and signature choices).
Make the decisions before generation, from the subject and the audience, not from the model's suggestions.
When a model proposes options, request deliberately different directions and add at least one of your own.
Compare the output with other generated pages before accepting it.
antiPatterns: Prompting 'make it modern and clean' and accepting the first result.
The same prompt and model as everyone else for the parts that carry identity.

howToCheck.machine: Compare the build's tokens (fonts, accent, radius, shadow) with a dated list of common generator defaults. Report the overlap.
howToCheck.human: Place the page among five generated pages. Can a newcomer pick it out and say why?

evidence.strengthNote: Doshi and Hauser (2024), Science Advances: writers given AI ideas wrote stories that were rated more creative and better written, especially the less creative writers, but the stories were more similar to each other. Holzner, Maier and Feuerriegel (2025; preprint): meta-analysis of 28 studies with 8,214 participants; people working with generative AI outperformed those without (g = 0.27), while idea diversity fell (g = -0.86). Wenger and Kenett (2025; preprint): responses of 22 LLMs on creativity tests were less varied than those of 102 humans. The evidence concerns text and ideas, not interface design, and two of the three sources are preprints.

sources.citation: Doshi, A. R., & Hauser, O. P. (2024). Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content. Science Advances, 10(28), eadn5290.
Holzner, N., Maier, S., & Feuerriegel, S. (2025). Generative AI and creativity: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis. arXiv:2505.17241 (preprint).
Wenger, E., & Kenett, Y. (2025). We're different, we're the same: Creative homogeneity across LLMs. arXiv:2501.19361 (preprint).

entries.caveats: Homogenization of ideas is shown. Homogenization of interfaces is inferred from it and from vendor observation (see ai-ui-default-cluster-drifts).
entries.sleekRelevance: States the generic problem in research terms: competent and convergent. The remedy the evidence points to is human decisions made before generation.

entries.principle: Generated interfaces cluster around a set of defaults, and the set changes
entries.claim: Model vendors report that LLM-built pages converge on recognizable defaults, and the named defaults shifted from Inter or system fonts and purple gradients on white (2025) to cream backgrounds with serif display type, terracotta accents and identical rounded cards (one vendor's list, late 2026). No peer-reviewed measurement of this convergence was found.
entries.mechanism: A model reproduces the most common patterns in its training data. When prompts are changed to avoid one cluster, the model settles on the next most probable cluster, which then becomes the new tell.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the defaults are usually usable
effects.satisfaction: unknown — untested for general users; design-aware viewers discount the look
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the defaults are conventional

designMoves: Check a build for unchosen defaults, not against a fixed blacklist: for each visual property, record whether a human Decision set it.
Keep the list of current tells as dated data and review it regularly.
Follow the brief even when it matches a listed tell; a deliberate choice is not a default.
Specify typeface, palette, radius, shadow, card treatment and label style explicitly in the build prompt.
antiPatterns: A fixed 'never use Inter or purple' rule treated as the solution.
One default look replaced with another fashionable one.
Any identity-carrying property left for the model to pick.

howToCheck.machine: Compare computed fonts, accent hue, gradients, radius, shadow and card patterns with a dated list of known generator defaults. Report which properties match and whether the Prescription specified them.
howToCheck.human: Does any element look as if nobody decided it?

evidence.strengthNote: Anthropic's cookbook on prompting for frontend aesthetics (2025) says that the model converges toward generic, 'on distribution' output, names Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts and purple gradients on white, and notes that the model then converged on another font. Anthropic's frontend-design skill, as revised on 3 September 2026, lists a different cluster (cream with a serif display face, terracotta accents, near-black with one acid-green accent, hairline 'broadsheet' layouts, identical rounded cards with one soft shadow, all-caps eyebrow labels, monospace data labels and others) and calls these defaults, not choices. Both were read in this session. OpenAI's GPT-5 frontend example notebook, also read, lists Inter among its recommended fonts, so vendor guidance conflicts. The story that Tailwind's default indigo seeded the purple habit rests on a 2025 social-media post by the framework's author, known here through secondary reports. HTTP Archive's 2025 Web Almanac puts Inter on roughly 1.4 to 1.5% of pages, so the impression that it is everywhere is specific to recent startup and generated sites.

OpenAI. GPT-5 frontend example notebook. openai-cookbook repository.
HTTP Archive (2025). Web Almanac 2025, Fonts chapter.
DEV Community post by the user 'alanwest' (2025). Why every AI-built website looks the same (blame Tailwind's indigo-500). Secondary report of the Tailwind author's post.

entries.caveats: This is vendor observation, not measurement. Whether ordinary users notice or penalize the look is untested. The lists describe particular models at particular times. The year of the DEV Community post is inferred from the event it reports.
entries.sleekRelevance: Central to the purpose of the tool: 'generic' is a moving target defined by what models currently default to. The durable test is whether each property was decided.

entries.principle: Seeing examples, especially AI-generated ones, narrows what people come up with
entries.claim: In one experiment, designers who used an AI image generator during ideation fixated more on an initial example and produced fewer ideas, with less variety and lower originality, than designers who worked without it.
entries.mechanism: Design fixation: once a concrete example is seen, its features anchor later ideas. Polished, high-fidelity examples anchor more strongly because they look finished.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — an example is easier than a blank page
effects.satisfaction: mixed — easier work, narrower results
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; the finding concerns the design process

designMoves: Form an intention (audience, personality, one signature idea) before looking at generated options.
Show options that differ on one variable at a time and that span a wide range, including an unexpected one.
Present early options at low fidelity (grayscale, structure only) so that they read as possibilities.
Record rejected options and the reasons, to keep later choices from drifting back to the first example.
antiPatterns: Starting from a generated mock-up and adjusting it.
Options that are near-duplicates.
Only high-fidelity previews at the first step.

howToCheck.machine: Measure the spread between the Options offered in a Step (distance between their token values). Flag Steps whose Options are too similar.
howToCheck.human: Before viewing options, write down the intended feel. Afterwards, check the pick against it.

evidence.strengthNote: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou and Velloso (2024), CHI: between-participants experiment, N = 60, a visual ideation task with or without an AI image generator; the AI group showed more fixation on an initial example and lower fluency, variety and originality. A single study with an early-generation tool; the authors note that results depend on how people prompt. Design fixation was first demonstrated by Jansson and Smith (1991), cited from memory.

sources.citation: Wadinambiarachchi, S., Kelly, R. M., Pareek, S., Zhou, Q., & Velloso, E. (2024). The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking. Proceedings of CHI 2024.
Jansson, D. G., & Smith, S. M. (1991). Design fixation. Design Studies, 12(1), 3-11.

entries.caveats: Examples also help novices who lack vocabulary; the cost is range. A step-by-step picker both benefits from this effect and is exposed to it.
entries.sleekRelevance: Bespoke results need an intention that precedes the examples. A picker that shows structure before decoration, and wide instead of similar options, works with this evidence.

entries.principle: What makes a design read as bespoke: specific content and visible decisions
entries.claim: No experiment was found that tests what makes an interface read as custom-made. The best-supported levers, by inference from adjacent research and from practitioner agreement, are subject-specific content and imagery, a deliberate typeface and palette, one distinctive element inside a conventional structure, and consistent fine detail.
entries.mechanism: Viewers infer effort and intent from specificity: things that could belong only to this subject, and choices that a default would not have produced. Generic content and default styling give no such evidence.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — as long as the structure stays conventional
effects.satisfaction: raises — by inference from the findings on typicality with novelty and on effort
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not tested; a bespoke identity should not alter how things work

designMoves: Write copy that names the actual product, audience and facts; remove sentences that could sit on any site.
Use real photographs, data and examples from the subject.
Open with the element most characteristic of the subject's world.
Choose one or two typefaces deliberately and set a clear scale.
Spend boldness on one memorable element; keep the rest disciplined.
Apply the craft-detail layer consistently (see invisible-details-craft-layer).
antiPatterns: Interchangeable headlines ('Build faster', 'Welcome to the future').
Feature grids of an icon in a rounded square with generic text.
Decoration added to simulate personality.

howToCheck.machine: Detect boilerplate and placeholder-like phrases. Check that typeface and accent differ from generator defaults and match the Prescription. Count signature elements (target: one).
howToCheck.human: Swap test: replace the logo and name with a competitor's. If the page still makes sense, it is not specific enough.

evidence.strengthNote: An inference from peer-reviewed work on typicality and novelty (Hekkert et al., 2003), effort and value (Kruger et al., 2004), attention to informative images (NN/g, 2010) and perceived craftsmanship (Moshagen and Thielsch, 2010), combined with vendor guidance read in this session (Anthropic's frontend-design skill: ground the design in the subject, choose typefaces deliberately, spend boldness on one memorable element). No direct test is known.

sources.citation: Anthropic (2026). frontend-design skill (SKILL.md, revision of 3 September 2026). anthropics/skills repository.

Hekkert, P., Snelders, D., & van Wieringen, P. C. W. (2003). 'Most advanced, yet acceptable': Typicality and novelty as joint predictors of aesthetic preference in industrial design. British Journal of Psychology, 94(1), 111-124.
Nielsen, J. (2010). Photos as web content. Nielsen Norman Group.

entries.caveats: What reads as bespoke to a designer and to a customer may differ. The swap test is a heuristic.
entries.sleekRelevance: This is the working definition of 'not generic' that the knowledge base can offer: nothing on the page is there by default, and something on it could belong to no one else.

entries.principle: Visual preferences differ by age, gender, education and country
entries.claim: In a study of about 2.4 million ratings from nearly 40,000 people, the preferred levels of colorfulness and visual complexity differed systematically by demographic group and by country. In related work, interfaces adapted to cultural preferences improved performance and satisfaction.
entries.mechanism: Taste is shaped by what people have seen most (media, local web conventions, education) and by perceptual changes that come with age. No single optimum suits everyone.

effects.cognitiveLoad: mixed — a density that suits one group burdens another
effects.satisfaction: raises — when the design matches the audience's preferred complexity and color
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — when local conventions are followed

designMoves: Name the audience (age range, region, education, familiarity with technology) before choosing density and colorfulness.
Do not take your own taste, or the taste of designers, for the audience's.
For international products, test visual options with people from each main market.
Where audiences are mixed, prefer moderate complexity and offer density or theme settings.
antiPatterns: One global design chosen by the team's taste.
The assumption that minimalism is preferred everywhere.
Stereotyping a culture from a single study.

howToCheck.human: Run a preference test of two or three visual directions with members of the intended audience.

evidence.strengthNote: Reinecke and Gajos (2014), CHI: about 2.4 million ratings of 430 website screenshots by almost 40,000 volunteers on an online research platform. Education correlated negatively with liking for colorful and complex sites; the paper reports that women liked more colorful designs than men; countries differed (for example, participants from Finland and Russia were among those most negatively affected by high complexity). Reinecke and Bernstein (2011): culturally adapted interfaces improved performance and satisfaction; the specific figures were not confirmed here. The volunteers were self-selected and the ratings were snap judgments of screenshots. Tractinsky et al. (2006) also note considerable individual differences.

sources.citation: Reinecke, K., & Gajos, K. Z. (2014). Quantifying visual preferences around the world. Proceedings of CHI 2014, 11-20.

Reinecke, K., & Bernstein, A. (2011). Improving performance, perceived usability, and aesthetics with culturally adaptive user interfaces. ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction, 18(2), Article 8.

entries.caveats: Group averages hide large individual variation. The data are from about 2012 and 2013; web conventions have converged since. The article number of the 2011 paper is recalled, not confirmed.
entries.sleekRelevance: 'Sleek' is itself a taste associated with particular audiences (educated, exposed to design). It is the right target when the audience shares it.

entries.principle: What looks right depends on the kind of site
entries.claim: People hold different expectations for different genres (shop, news, company site, app): where things are, how dense the page is, which look fits. A design is judged against the prototype of its own genre.
entries.mechanism: People learn a prototype for each category. Fit with the prototype makes a page easy to process and credible for its purpose; a mismatch (a bank that looks like a game) creates doubt before any content is read.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — placement and density typical of the genre match expectations
effects.satisfaction: raises — fit reads as competence
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — the conventions of the genre apply

designMoves: Identify the genre and collect several respected examples that the audience knows.
List what those examples share (layout, density, tone); keep these unless there is a reason not to.
Choose density by genre: operational tools are dense, marketing pages are spacious.
Borrow from another genre only as a deliberate signature.
antiPatterns: The spaciousness of a marketing page applied to a data-heavy tool.
Playful styling in a high-stakes domain without intent.
One template for every type of project.

howToCheck.machine: Compare density measures (elements per viewport, text size, row height) with reference ranges for each Template family.
howToCheck.human: Ask a newcomer, after a look of a few seconds, what kind of organization this is.

evidence.strengthNote: Roth et al. (2010) compared users' location expectations across online shops, news portals and company pages. Tuch et al. (2012) defined prototypicality relative to the category of website. The guidance on density by genre is practitioner inference, not a tested result.

sources.citation: Roth, S. P., Schmutz, P., Pauwels, S. L., Bargas-Avila, J. A., & Opwis, K. (2010). Mental models for web objects: Where do users expect to find the most frequent objects in online shops, news portals, and company web pages? Interacting with Computers, 22(2), 140-152.

Tuch, A. N., Presslaber, E. E., Stöcklin, M., Opwis, K., & Bargas-Avila, J. A. (2012). The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 70(11), 794-811.

entries.caveats: Genres blur and evolve, and leading products reset the prototype for their genre.
entries.sleekRelevance: The most admired products are exemplary members of their genre before they are original.

entries.principle: Following accessibility guidelines improves performance and ratings for non-disabled users too
entries.claim: In controlled experiments, websites built to higher accessibility conformance were used with better performance and were rated more usable and more attractive by people without disabilities.
entries.mechanism: Accessibility guidelines encode general good practice: sufficient contrast, clear structure, labeled controls, predictable behavior, help with errors. These lower effort for everyone, most noticeably under constraint (small screens, glare, hurry, age).

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — clearer structure and labels
effects.satisfaction: raises — higher usability and aesthetics ratings in the experiments
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — labeled, predictable controls

designMoves: Treat the accessibility baseline (WCAG 2.x Level AA) as a quality requirement for all users.
Run automated checks on every build and fix what they find.
Add the manual checks that tools cannot do: keyboard-only use, a screen-reader pass, enlarged text, readable link and button names.
Where the product matters to people with disabilities, complement conformance checks with testing by them.
antiPatterns: Accessibility treated as a late compliance task.
Overlay widgets in place of fixes.
Declaring the job done after automated checks pass.

howToCheck.machine: Run axe-core or a similar engine and assert zero violations for the chosen rule set; check contrast, labels, landmarks and focus order.
howToCheck.human: Complete the main task with the keyboard only, and again with a screen reader.

evidence.strengthNote: Schmutz, Sonderegger and Sauer (2016), Human Factors: 61 non-disabled participants used versions of a site at three levels of WCAG 2.0 conformance; higher conformance gave better performance and more positive ratings, including perceived usability and aesthetics. A 2017 study by the same authors found no interaction between user group (with or without visual impairment) and accessibility level. Vollenwyder et al. (2023): 66 participants with visual impairments and 65 without used a shop with low or high conformance; the conformant shop was associated with more positive experiences for the first group and fewer negative experiences for the second, and the authors caution that conformance alone is not sufficient. One research group produced the 2016 and 2017 studies.

sources.citation: Schmutz, S., Sonderegger, A., & Sauer, J. (2016). Implementing recommendations from Web Accessibility Guidelines: Would they also provide benefits to nondisabled users. Human Factors, 58(4), 611-629.

Vollenwyder, B., Petralito, S., Iten, G. H., Brühlmann, F., Opwis, K., & Mekler, E. D. (2023). How compliance with web accessibility standards shapes the experiences of users with and without disabilities. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies, 170, 102956.

entries.caveats: Automated tools detect only a portion of accessibility problems. Passing checks is not a claim of conformance: state what was checked and what a person must still check.
entries.sleekRelevance: Accessibility and refinement share most of their means: contrast, clarity, structure, predictability. An elegant look that fails them is elegant for fewer people and, by this evidence, is rated lower even by those it does not exclude.

entries.principle: Accessibility is a legal baseline that most sites still miss
entries.claim: Automated testing of the top one million home pages in 2026 found detectable accessibility failures on about 96% of them, with low-contrast text the most common. Accessibility is a legal requirement in a growing number of settings: US state and local government sites must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA under a 2024 rule (first deadlines extended to 2027 and 2028), and European Union rules for many consumer products and services have been enforced since 2025.
entries.mechanism: Failures persist because the defaults of popular tools fail (low-contrast grays, unlabeled icons), because the problems are invisible to those who do not experience them, and because checks are left to the end.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — once the common failures are fixed
effects.satisfaction: raises — most for excluded users, and for others too
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: raises — labels and structure help everyone

designMoves: Meet the contrast minimums for all text and controls in every theme and state.
Give every image a text alternative and every form control a label.
Give every link and button a discernible name.
Check generated code specifically: the common failures are the ones that generators reproduce.
Record what was checked, how and when.
antiPatterns: Light gray text on white for elegance.
Icon-only buttons without accessible names.
Placeholder text as the only label.
A claim of compliance based on an automated scan.

howToCheck.machine: Scan automatically for the most common failure types in the WebAIM analysis: low-contrast text, missing alternative text, missing form labels, empty links and empty buttons.
howToCheck.human: Review by hand what tools cannot judge: whether alternative text is meaningful, focus order, help with errors.

evidence.strengthNote: Law: the US Department of Justice rule under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (2024) adopts WCAG 2.1 Level AA; an interim final rule of April 2026 moved the compliance dates to April 2027 for larger entities and April 2028 for smaller ones, and that extension is under legal challenge. These points come from law-firm summaries, not from the primary text. The European Accessibility Act date rests on a search result and on memory. Prevalence: the WebAIM Million 2026 analysis reports detected WCAG failures on 95.9% of home pages (94.8% in 2025), an average of 56.1 errors per page, and low-contrast text on 83.9%; the figures are from secondary coverage because the WebAIM site could not be reached in this session. Automated detection understates the true failure rate.

sources.citation: WebAIM (2026). The WebAIM Million: The 2026 report on the accessibility of the top 1,000,000 home pages.
US Department of Justice. ADA Title II web and mobile accessibility rule (2024) and interim final rule extending compliance dates (April 2026).
Jackson Lewis (2026). DOJ extends public entities' compliance deadline for ADA-related website accessibility.
Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act).

entries.caveats: Laws differ by country and sector, and they change. This entry is not legal advice. Duties of private businesses in the United States rest on other provisions and on case law.
entries.sleekRelevance: Since nearly every site fails the basics, meeting them is a real differentiator. Low-contrast 'elegance' is the single most common failure.

entries.principle: Let people stop motion
entries.claim: Moving content that starts by itself, lasts more than five seconds and appears alongside other content must be pausable, and the strictest level of the guidelines asks that animation triggered by interaction can be disabled. Motion can cause dizziness, nausea and headaches for people with vestibular disorders.
entries.mechanism: The vestibular system (the balance sense of the inner ear) can be disturbed by on-screen movement that does not match the body's motion, which produces physical symptoms. Moving content also pulls attention from reading.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer distractions
effects.satisfaction: raises — decisively for affected users
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured; states without motion must still show changes clearly

designMoves: Honor the prefers-reduced-motion setting: replace movement with a fade or an instant change.
Provide a pause, stop or hide control for any movement that starts by itself and runs longer than five seconds.
Avoid parallax, large zooms and scroll-jacking; if they are used, remove them under reduced motion.
Never rely on animation alone to convey that something changed.
antiPatterns: Background video that plays by itself with no pause control.
Parallax and scroll-triggered movement with no reduced-motion variant.
Endless decorative animation next to text.

howToCheck.machine: Emulate 'prefers-reduced-motion: reduce' and assert that animations and transitions are removed or shortened. Detect animations that run longer than five seconds without a pause control. Detect video that plays automatically.
howToCheck.human: Enable 'reduce motion' in the operating system and use the product.

evidence.strengthNote: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) and 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (Level AAA), with the W3C explanatory document that describes vestibular reactions; all were read from the W3C source in this session. Level AAA criteria are not required by most laws; support for the reduce-motion preference is common practice in design systems.

sources.citation: W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, Success Criterion 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.
W3C. Understanding Success Criterion 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions. Source file in the w3c/wcag repository.

entries.caveats: Reduced motion does not mean no feedback: keep changes of state visible.
entries.sleekRelevance: A product that respects system preferences without being asked feels considerate, and that is part of feeling well made.
